name: Bronze Age Dawn
desc: The first city-states rise along the great river valleys. Writing emerges. Empire is being invented.

events.name: Invention of Cuneiform
events.desc: At Uruk, the first writing system is developed — wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets, initially for administrative accounting of grain and livestock. Over the next millennium it will expand into literature, law, and diplomacy.

events.name: Construction of Stonehenge
events.desc: The first phase of Stonehenge is built on Salisbury Plain — a circular earthwork enclosure. The great sarsen stones arrive roughly 500 years later. A monument older than the Pyramids.

events.name: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
events.desc: Traditionally credited to King Narmer, the unification of the Two Lands creates the first territorial nation-state in history. The capital at Memphis, founded at the head of the Delta, will anchor Egyptian civilization for 3,000 years.

polities.name: Sumer
polities.desc: The earliest civilization on the alluvial plain between the Tigris and Euphrates. Cuneiform, the wheel, and the first codified law trace their origins here.
polities.note: From Sumerian temple economies emerges every later notion of bureaucratic governance.

polities.name: Old Kingdom Egypt
polities.desc: The Nile valley unified under pharaonic rule. The pyramids at Giza date to this era — engineering monuments to a centralized theocratic state.
polities.note: Geographic determinism in pure form: a river, a desert, a god-king.

polities.name: Indus Valley
polities.desc: Planned cities with grid streets, drainage, and standardized weights. Script remains undeciphered. Trade extended to Mesopotamia.

polities.name: Early Dynastic China
polities.desc: Bronze metallurgy and ritual vessels mark the emergence of stratified society along the Yellow River.

name: Classical World
desc: Persia rules from the Indus to the Aegean. Greek city-states resist. Confucius and the Buddha are recently dead. Rome is a small republic.

events.name: Battle of Marathon
events.desc: An Athenian hoplite force of ~10,000 defeats a Persian invasion army roughly twice its size. The runner Pheidippides carries the news to Athens. The victory preserves Greek political independence and, with it, the intellectual tradition that will shape the West.

events.name: Death of Confucius
events.desc: Confucius dies at Qufu after decades of teaching in a China divided among warring states. The system of ethics, ritual, and political philosophy he leaves behind will dominate East Asian thought for 2,500 years.

events.name: Death of the Buddha
events.desc: Siddhartha Gautama dies at Kushinagar. His teaching spreads through the subcontinent under Ashoka two centuries later, then eastward along the Silk Road into China, Korea, and Japan.

events.name: Founding of the Roman Republic
events.desc: Rome expels Tarquinius Superbus, its last king, and establishes a republic of consuls, Senate, and popular assemblies. The constitutional framework will outlast Rome itself — every later republic from Venice to the United States draws on its vocabulary.

events.name: Alexander the Great — greatest extent
events.desc: Alexander III of Macedon dies of fever in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in Babylon at thirty-two. In twelve years he has destroyed the Achaemenid Empire, conquered from the Aegean to the Indus, and founded some twenty cities named after himself. The empire fractures among his generals within a generation — the Seleucids in Asia, the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Antigonids in Macedon — but the Hellenistic world he created will persist for three centuries, transmitting Greek language, philosophy, and urban form from Egypt to Afghanistan. The Septuagint, the New Testament's Greek, and the Gandharan Buddhas all grow out of his wake.

polities.name: Achaemenid Persia
polities.desc: The first empire on a continental scale. Cyrus and Darius built a system of satrapies, royal roads, and tolerant administration that became the template every later empire would either imitate or oppose.
polities.note: The Persians invented the imperial form. Everything after — Hellenistic, Roman, even Islamic caliphates — sits in their structural shadow.

polities.name: Greek Poleis
polities.desc: Hundreds of independent city-states sharing language and gods. The cradle of philosophy, drama, and the conceptual vocabulary the West still uses to think.

polities.name: Roman Republic
polities.desc: A regional Italian power, recently expelled its kings, beginning the long wars with Carthage and the Italian peninsula.

polities.name: Magadha / Early Mauryan
polities.desc: The Magadha kingdom that would, within two centuries, become Ashoka's empire spanning most of the subcontinent.

polities.name: Zhou China (Warring States)
polities.desc: The nominal Zhou dynasty has dissolved into seven warring kingdoms — Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao, Wei — contesting the North China Plain. From this crucible emerges Confucianism, Daoism, and Legalism. The south (Guangdong, Yunnan, Fujian) is considered barbarian territory.

name: The Ides of March
desc: Julius Caesar is assassinated by senators in the Theatre of Pompey. Within a generation the Republic will be gone, replaced by Augustus and the principate. The hinge between republican and imperial Rome.

events.name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.desc: On the Ides of March, 44 BC, Caesar is stabbed 23 times by a conspiracy of senators at the foot of Pompey's statue in the Theatre of Pompey. The conspirators hope to restore the Republic. Instead they trigger thirteen more years of civil war ending with Augustus as emperor.

events.name: Crossing of the Rubicon
events.desc: Caesar leads the 13th Legion across the Rubicon, a small river marking the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper. The act is constitutionally treasonous. Alea iacta est — the die is cast.

events.name: Battle of Carrhae
events.desc: Crassus, seeking glory equal to Caesar's and Pompey's, leads seven Roman legions into Parthian territory. Parthian horse archers annihilate them. Crassus is killed; molten gold reportedly poured down his throat. The Euphrates becomes Rome's permanent eastern limit.

polities.name: Roman Republic (terminal)
polities.desc: The Republic has swallowed the Mediterranean but cannot govern it. Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BC ended the constitutional order; his assassination will not restore it. Octavian and Antony will divide the inheritance and then fight over it.
polities.note: Every later transition from republic to empire — French, American, any future case — is measured against this one.

polities.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
polities.desc: Cleopatra VII rules the last independent Hellenistic kingdom. Her alliance with Caesar produced a son; her alliance with Antony will end at Actium in 31 BC. Egypt will then become a Roman province of the emperor personally.

polities.name: Parthian Empire
polities.desc: Rome's great eastern rival. Crassus died at Carrhae in 53 BC trying to conquer them. The Euphrates will remain the eastern limit of Roman power for three centuries.

polities.name: Nabataean Kingdom
polities.desc: Arab kingdom controlling the caravan trade between Arabia and the Mediterranean from its rock-cut capital at Petra. Nominally independent, walks a careful line between Rome and Parthia. Will be annexed by Trajan in 106 AD.

polities.name: Mauretania (client kingdom)
polities.desc: Berber kingdom west of Roman Africa, under the rule of client kings installed by Rome. Juba II will marry Cleopatra's daughter Selene. Annexed as a Roman province under Claudius in 44 AD.

polities.name: Han China
polities.desc: Emperor Yuan of Han rules. The dynasty is past its expansionist peak under Wu but the Silk Road is active — Roman glass reaches China, Chinese silk reaches Rome, though neither empire knows the other exists as anything but a rumor. Han rules China proper and holds protectorates over the Tarim Basin, but has no direct control over Tibet, Mongolia, or Manchuria.

polities.name: Mauryan Successors
polities.desc: The Mauryan Empire has been gone for 140 years. The subcontinent is divided among Shunga, Satavahana, Indo-Greek, and other successor kingdoms. A period of political fragmentation and religious ferment.

polities.name: Celtic Britain & Ireland
polities.desc: Caesar's two expeditions in 55 and 54 BC were shows of force, not conquest — he extracted tribute and left. In 44 BC the island is still ruled by Iron-Age tribal confederations: Catuvellauni, Trinovantes, Iceni, Brigantes, Silures, Caledonians, Picts. Druids control the religious life; oppida (hillfort towns) are the political centers. Ireland, never invaded by Rome, will remain Celtic until the fifth century. Claudius's permanent invasion of Britain is still 87 years away.

name: Pax Romana
desc: Rome reaches its territorial peak under Trajan. The Mediterranean is a Roman lake. Han China rules the East. Two empires, no contact, governing perhaps half of humanity.

events.name: Death of Trajan
events.desc: Trajan dies at Selinus in Cilicia, returning from his Parthian campaign. He leaves the empire at its maximum territorial extent. His successor Hadrian will immediately abandon Mesopotamia, judging it indefensible — the first time the empire formally contracts.

events.name: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.desc: Vesuvius erupts on August 24 (traditional date), burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under volcanic ash. The eruption kills perhaps 16,000 and preserves, in near-perfect condition, a snapshot of Roman daily life that archaeology would begin excavating 1,700 years later.

events.name: Invention of Paper
events.desc: The Han court official Cai Lun presents a process for making paper from tree bark, hemp, and old rags. The invention will take a thousand years to reach Europe but will, when it does, make printing economically feasible.

polities.name: Roman Empire (Trajan)
polities.desc: From Britannia to Mesopotamia. The greatest territorial extent Rome would ever achieve. A single legal system, a common elite language, roads from York to Damascus.
polities.note: One of the only true thalassocratic empires in history — the sea, not the land, was the spine.

polities.name: Han China
polities.desc: Contemporary with Rome and roughly equal in scale. Invented paper, the seismograph, and the civil service examination. Silk Road trade indirectly connected the two empires. Han controls China proper south to the Red River delta, plus protectorates over the Tarim Basin.

polities.name: Parthian Empire
polities.desc: Rome's eastern adversary. Parthian cavalry destroyed Crassus at Carrhae. The empire that prevented Roman expansion past the Euphrates.

polities.name: Kushan Empire
polities.desc: Central Asian dynasty controlling the Silk Road's middle passage. Patron of Buddhist art and the bridge between Mediterranean and Chinese trade.

name: Fall of Rome
desc: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western emperor. The eastern half continues for another thousand years from Constantinople. What dies here is a specific political arrangement; what survives is the civilizational memory that will drive European history for the next fifteen centuries.

events.name: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.desc: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the 16-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople, declaring that the West needed no emperor. The Senate continues to meet for another century, but the Western Empire is administratively finished.

events.name: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.desc: Alaric's Visigoths enter Rome and sack the city for three days. The symbolic blow is greater than the material damage — the city has not been taken by a foreign enemy in 800 years. Augustine's *City of God* is written in response.

events.name: Baptism of Clovis
events.desc: The Frankish king Clovis is baptized at Reims by Bishop Remigius. The first Germanic king to convert to Nicene Christianity rather than Arianism, the act aligns the Franks with the Roman Church and sets the foundation for medieval Western Christendom.

polities.name: Eastern Roman Empire
polities.desc: The empire that did not fall. Zeno rules from Constantinople; the eastern Mediterranean remains intact. Justinian's reconquest of Italy and North Africa is sixty years away.
polities.note: The continuous operation of the Roman state for another millennium is one of the most underrated facts in world history.

polities.name: Kingdom of the Ostrogoths
polities.desc: Within a generation Theodoric will rule Italy as a Roman-style king, preserving senatorial institutions and infrastructure while the Ostrogoths provide military power. A brief attempt to keep the Roman administrative machine running under new management.

polities.name: Kingdom of the Franks
polities.desc: Clovis is consolidating power in Gaul. His conversion to Nicene Christianity in 496 will align the Franks with the Roman Church and set the stage for Charlemagne three centuries later.

polities.name: Visigothic Kingdom
polities.desc: Ruling most of Iberia and southwestern Gaul. The Franks will push them out of Gaul; the Umayyads will end the kingdom entirely in 711.

polities.name: Vandal Kingdom
polities.desc: Geiseric's Vandals control North Africa and the western Mediterranean, having sacked Rome in 455. Justinian will destroy them in the 530s.

polities.name: Sassanid Persia
polities.desc: The great Eastern rival. At roughly equivalent power with the Eastern Romans. Both empires will exhaust each other in the early 7th century, opening the way for the Arab conquests.

polities.name: Gupta India (declining)
polities.desc: The Gupta 'Golden Age' is ending under Hun pressure. Classical Sanskrit literature, mathematics, and astronomy reach their peak just as the political order that supported them dissolves.

polities.name: Northern Wei China
polities.desc: A Xianbei dynasty ruling northern China, sinicizing rapidly. The southern dynasties rule from Jiankang. The long division that began with Han's collapse continues. Northern Wei controls the northern half of China proper — the Yellow River basin and the Yangtze's northern bank.

name: Rise of the Caliphate
desc: Twenty-five years of war between Byzantium and Persia end in 628 with both empires exhausted. Within a decade, armies from Medina break them both at Yarmouk and al-Qadisiyyah in 636.

events.name: Death of Muhammad
events.desc: Muhammad dies at Medina in June 632, ten years after the Hijra. Abu Bakr becomes the first caliph and spends two years bringing the Arabian tribes back under Medina.

events.name: Battle of the Yarmuk
events.desc: In August 636 a Rashidun army routs Heraclius' field army on the Yarmouk river. Byzantine rule in Syria effectively ends.

events.name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.desc: In November 636 Arab forces beat the Sasanian army near al-Hira. Iraq lies open, and the capital Ctesiphon falls the next year.

events.name: Surrender of Jerusalem to Caliph Umar
events.desc: After a six-month siege, Patriarch Sophronius surrenders Jerusalem on condition that he submit to the caliph himself. Umar comes in person in 637 or 638.

events.name: Arab conquest of Egypt
events.desc: Amr ibn al-As invades Egypt in 639. Babylon fortress falls in 641 and Alexandria by treaty; Byzantine troops leave in 642, ending seven centuries of Roman Egypt.

events.name: Battle of Nahavand
events.desc: Yazdegerd III's last great army is destroyed in the Zagros in 642. He flees east and is killed near Merv in 651, ending the Sasanian dynasty.

polities.name: Rashidun Caliphate
polities.desc: Four years after Muhammad's death, the caliph Umar's armies hold Arabia and are taking Syria and Palestine. Yarmouk and al-Qadisiyyah, both fought in 636, decide the next decade.
polities.note: Syria and Palestine are shown with the Caliphate because Yarmouk (August 636) ended Byzantine rule there. Jerusalem held out until 637 or 638, and Caesarea until 640 or 641.

polities.name: Byzantine Empire
polities.desc: Heraclius beat Persia in 628 and recovered the True Cross, then lost Syria to the Arabs eight years later. Egypt, Anatolia, the coasts of Africa and Italy remain Roman.
polities.note: Includes the Exarchate of Africa (Carthage) and client princes in Armenia and Lazica. The Exarchate of Ravenna, Rome, Sicily and the far south of Italy were also Byzantine; Italy is filled with the Lombards because the map cannot split it.

polities.name: Sasanian Empire
polities.desc: Exhausted by the war of 602-628 and a string of short reigns, Persia crowns the boy-king Yazdegerd III in 632. It loses al-Qadisiyyah in 636, Ctesiphon in 637 and Nahavand in 642.

polities.name: Western Turkic Khaganate
polities.desc: Overlords of the Silk Road oases from the Altai to Tokharistan, ruling through Sogdian city-states and local yabghus. Civil war after 630 is weakening it.
polities.note: Turfan (Gaochang) and the Tarim oases are shown here; Tang took Gaochang in 640.

polities.name: Tang China
polities.desc: Emperor Taizong has reunified China and destroyed the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630. Chang'an is probably the largest city on earth.
polities.note: Northern Vietnam is the Tang protectorate of Jiaozhou (later Annan); the Mekong delta is shown with Funan's successors under Vietnam's single shape.

polities.name: Tibetan Empire
polities.desc: Songtsen Gampo has united the plateau. His marriage to the Tang princess Wencheng in 641 will bring Buddhism and Chinese writing into court life.

polities.name: Goguryeo
polities.desc: The northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, holding Manchuria and the north of the peninsula. It beat off Sui invasions in 612 and will face Tang ones from 645.

polities.name: Silla and Baekje
polities.desc: The two southern Korean kingdoms, at war with each other. Silla's alliance with Tang will destroy Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.

polities.name: Yamato Japan
polities.desc: The Asuka court under Emperor Jomei sent its first embassy to Tang in 630. The Taika reforms of 645 are nine years away.

polities.name: Harsha's empire
polities.desc: Harsha rules the Ganges plain from Kanauj and hosts the pilgrim Xuanzang. The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II stopped him at the Narmada; Pallavas hold the far south.
polities.note: India is one shape on this map, so the Chalukya and Pallava south is filled with Harsha's north.

polities.name: Kingdom of Sindh (Rai and Brahman dynasties)
polities.desc: The Brahman dynasty has just replaced the Rai kings of Sindh. Kabul and Zabul to the north are ruled by Turk and Hephthalite princes.

polities.name: Anuradhapura Kingdom
polities.desc: Sri Lanka's Buddhist kingdom, a hub of the Indian Ocean trade between Persia, India and China.

polities.name: Visigothic Kingdom
polities.desc: Christian, Catholic since 589, and ruling all of Iberia since the last Byzantine towns fell around 625. Toledo's church councils double as its parliament.
polities.note: Includes Septimania, the strip of southern France from the Pyrenees to the Rhône.

polities.name: Merovingian Franks
polities.desc: Dagobert I is the last strong Merovingian king, ruling Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy together and holding the Alamanni, Thuringians and Bavarians as subjects.

polities.name: Lombard Kingdom
polities.desc: The Lombards have held the Po valley and the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento since 568. Rotharis will issue their first written law code in 643.
polities.note: Italy is filled with the Lombards; Ravenna, Rome, Naples, Sicily and the toe and heel of Italy stayed Byzantine.

polities.name: Samo's realm
polities.desc: A Frankish merchant leads the western Slavs against the Avars and beats Dagobert's army at Wogastisburg around 631.

polities.name: Avar Khaganate
polities.desc: Steppe overlords of Pannonia and the Danube plain. Their failed siege of Constantinople in 626 broke their power over the Balkan Slavs.

polities.name: Kingdom of Aksum
polities.desc: The Christian kingdom of the Ethiopian highlands, past its peak. It sheltered Muhammad's followers in the first Hijra of 615.

polities.name: Nubian kingdoms (Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia)
polities.desc: Three Christian kingdoms on the middle Nile. Makuria will beat an Arab army at Dongola in 652 and win a treaty that lasts six centuries.

polities.name: East African farmers, herders and coastal traders
Yunnan chiefdoms (Cuan and the six zhao)
Chenla, Dvaravati, Pyu and island kingdoms
Classic Maya city-states and late Teotihuacan

name: Carolingian World
desc: Charlemagne is crowned in Rome. The Abbasid Caliphate rules from Spain to Central Asia. Tang China is the wealthiest civilization on earth. Constantinople holds.

events.name: Coronation of Charlemagne
events.desc: On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne 'Emperor of the Romans' at Old St. Peter's Basilica. The act revives the Western imperial title dormant since 476 and creates the political-theological framework of Latin Christendom for the next thousand years.

events.name: Founding of the House of Wisdom
events.desc: The Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun formalizes a library and translation academy at Baghdad. Scholars translate Greek philosophical, medical, and mathematical works into Arabic, preserving texts that would otherwise have been lost and extending them further.

events.name: Founding of Viking Dublin
events.desc: Norse raiders establish a longphort — a fortified ship encampment — at the mouth of the Liffey. It will grow into Dublin. The Viking age is transforming Europe's coasts from Ireland to the Black Sea.

polities.name: Carolingian Empire
polities.desc: Charlemagne's restoration of the Western Empire. The cultural foundation of what would become Latin Christendom — and, eventually, Europe.
polities.note: The first deliberate attempt to recover the Roman idea after its collapse. The template for every later European unification project.

polities.name: Abbasid Caliphate
polities.desc: The golden age of Islamic civilization. Baghdad's House of Wisdom preserved and extended Greek philosophy, mathematics, and medicine while Europe was largely illiterate.

polities.name: Byzantine Empire
polities.desc: The Roman Empire that never fell. By 800 reduced to Anatolia, the Balkans, and southern Italy, but still the wealthiest and most sophisticated state in Christendom.

polities.name: Tang China
polities.desc: Cosmopolitan empire of perhaps 50 million people. Chang'an may have been the largest city on earth. Buddhism, poetry, and printing flourished. Tang at 800 is past its territorial peak — the An Lushan rebellion (755-763) has cost it Central Asia — but still controls China proper and the Gansu corridor.

polities.name: Kingdom of Asturias
polities.desc: The northern Christian remnant after the Umayyad conquest of Iberia. The seed of the Reconquista.

name: Height of the Crusades
desc: Jerusalem falls to the First Crusade after a five-week siege. For the first time since the 7th century, the Holy Land is under Christian rule. The Crusader states will last two centuries; the theological, military, and commercial consequences will last much longer.

events.name: Siege of Jerusalem
events.desc: After a five-week siege and a massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish populations, the First Crusade's army takes Jerusalem on July 15, 1099. Godfrey of Bouillon becomes Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre. The Kingdom of Jerusalem is founded.

events.name: Council of Clermont
events.desc: Pope Urban II preaches the First Crusade, calling on Western Christendom to aid the Byzantines and recover Jerusalem. The speech — of which no transcript survives — becomes the most consequential papal address in medieval history.

events.name: Battle of Manzikert
events.desc: The Seljuk Turks destroy the Byzantine field army and capture Emperor Romanos IV. Anatolia — the empire's demographic and military heartland — is lost. The Byzantine appeal for Western help that follows will produce the First Crusade.

polities.name: Crusader States
polities.desc: The Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch, the County of Edessa, and the County of Tripoli — four Latin polities carved from the coastal Levant. Defended by a few thousand knights in a sea of hostile population.
polities.note: The Crusades inaugurated the first sustained contact between Latin Christendom and the Islamic world. Banking, algebra, paper, the compass, and much of classical philosophy returned west through these conduits.

polities.name: Byzantine Empire (Komnenian revival)
polities.desc: Alexios I Komnenos called for Western help against the Seljuks and got the Crusade he did not expect. The empire is recovering; the Crusaders are at once allies, rivals, and — in 1204 — the force that will sack Constantinople itself.

polities.name: Fatimid Caliphate
polities.desc: The Ismaili Shia caliphate controlling Egypt and, until its loss to the Crusaders this year, much of the Levantine coast. Will fall to Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty in 1171.

polities.name: Great Seljuk Empire
polities.desc: The Turkic dynasty that took Baghdad in 1055 and broke Byzantine power at Manzikert in 1071. Fragmenting now into regional atabegs, which is precisely why the First Crusade succeeded.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.desc: Henry IV is Emperor, exhausted by decades of conflict with the papacy over investiture. The German princes are consolidating autonomy; the outlines of a patchwork empire are hardening.

polities.name: Kingdom of France (Capetian)
polities.desc: Philip I reigns but his actual domain is tiny — a patch of royal land around Paris. The great lords of France provided most of the Crusading manpower.

polities.name: Norman Kingdoms
polities.desc: The Normans rule England (since 1066), southern Italy, and Sicily. The most dynamic military culture in Europe, and a major source of Crusading leadership — Bohemond of Antioch is a Norman.

polities.name: Almoravid Empire
polities.desc: Berber dynasty from the Sahara that unified Morocco and crossed into Iberia in 1086, halting the Reconquista. At its peak around this moment.

polities.name: Song China
polities.desc: The Northern Song reigns over a commercial, literary, and technological boom — paper money, gunpowder weapons, porcelain, movable type. The richest civilization on earth. The Khitan Liao holds the sixteen prefectures around modern Beijing; the Jurchen will sack Kaifeng in twenty-eight years.

polities.name: Chola Empire
polities.desc: Tamil thalassocracy whose navy has just raided Srivijaya in Sumatra. The dominant power in south India and the Indian Ocean.

polities.name: Kingdom of Ghana
polities.desc: West African empire controlling the trans-Saharan gold trade. Being pressured by the Almoravids; will give way to Mali within a century.

name: Mongol Century
desc: The largest contiguous land empire in history. From Korea to Hungary under one Khan. The Pax Mongolica re-opens Eurasian trade. Marco Polo is in Beijing.

events.name: Marco Polo at the Yuan Court
events.desc: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo arrives at Khanbaliq (modern Beijing) and enters the service of Kublai Khan. His account on returning to Venice will introduce Europe to Chinese paper money, coal, porcelain, and the scale of Asian wealth.

events.name: Mongol Sack of Baghdad
events.desc: Hulagu Khan's army takes Baghdad after a twelve-day siege. The last Abbasid caliph is executed; the House of Wisdom's library is thrown into the Tigris; perhaps 200,000 are killed. The symbolic center of Islamic civilization for five centuries is destroyed.

events.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
events.desc: The Mamluks of Egypt under Sultan Qutuz defeat a Mongol army at Ain Jalut in Palestine. The first significant Mongol defeat; the event that fixes the Euphrates as the western limit of Mongol power and preserves the Islamic heartland.

events.name: Founding of Yuan Dynasty
events.desc: Kublai Khan formally proclaims the Yuan dynasty, the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China. He moves the capital from Karakorum to Dadu (Beijing) and adopts Chinese administrative forms.

events.name: Yuan court makes Zhu Xi's Four Books the civil service exam canon
events.desc: A 1313 Yuan decree revived the civil service exams, first held in 1315, with Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Four Books as the standard. Neo-Confucian orthodoxy then set China's exams until 1905.

polities.name: Mongol Empire (Yuan + Khanates)
polities.desc: By 1300, formally divided into four khanates: the Yuan in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Chagatai in Central Asia, and the Golden Horde in the western steppe. Together still the largest political entity ever.
polities.note: The Mongols compressed Eurasia. The Black Death, gunpowder, and the printing press all traveled the routes they secured.

polities.name: Mamluk Sultanate
polities.desc: The slave-soldier dynasty that broke the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut and ended the Crusader states. Ruled Egypt and the Levant.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.desc: Voltaire's quip — neither holy, Roman, nor an empire — applies. A patchwork of duchies, free cities, and bishoprics under a notional emperor.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.desc: Philip IV is consolidating royal power, taxing the clergy, and about to dissolve the Knights Templar. The early architecture of the modern state.

polities.name: Delhi Sultanate
polities.desc: Turkic-Persian Muslim dynasty controlling most of north India. The Khalji dynasty under Alauddin is at its peak.

name: Fall of Constantinople
desc: Mehmed II takes Constantinople after a fifty-three-day siege, ending the Roman Empire's eleven-century continuous existence. The Ottomans now command the land bridge between Europe and Asia. Greek scholars flee west with manuscripts, feeding the Italian Renaissance.

events.name: Fall of Constantinople
events.desc: On May 29, 1453, after a fifty-three-day siege featuring the largest cannon ever built to that point, Ottoman forces breach the Theodosian walls. Emperor Constantine XI dies in the fighting. Mehmed II, twenty-one years old, rides into Hagia Sophia. The Roman Empire ends after 2,206 years.

events.name: Gutenberg's Printing Press
events.desc: Johannes Gutenberg develops movable-type printing in Mainz. The Gutenberg Bible appears around 1455. Within fifty years, more than twenty million books will be printed in Europe — more than were produced in the preceding thousand years of manuscript copying.

events.name: End of the Hundred Years' War
events.desc: The Battle of Castillon, the last major engagement of the Hundred Years' War, ends English territorial claims in France save Calais. The same year Constantinople falls; an era closes across Europe simultaneously.

events.name: Ivan III faces down the Great Horde at the Ugra River
events.desc: Akhmat Khan's army faced Ivan III's across the Ugra in autumn 1480, then withdrew without a major battle. Russian historians date the end of the Tatar yoke from it, though some doubt it changed much.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire (Mehmed II)
polities.desc: The conquering sultan styles himself 'Kayser-i Rum' — Caesar of Rome. The Ottomans now straddle Europe and Asia; the Balkans and Anatolia are theirs; Egypt, Hungary, and Vienna will follow over the next eighty years.
polities.note: The event that drove Europeans to seek sea routes to Asia — directly causing Columbus's voyage thirty-nine years later.

polities.name: Timurid Empire (fragmenting)
polities.desc: Tamerlane's empire, fifty years after his death, is splitting among his descendants. The Timurid cultural renaissance under Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg reaches its peak just as the political structure dissolves.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.desc: Charles VII has just won the Hundred Years' War — English troops left France in 1453 as well. The royal domain is being consolidated; the modern French state is emerging.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.desc: Henry VI's government is failing. The Wars of the Roses will begin in two years. England has lost all its French possessions except Calais.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.desc: Frederick III has been Emperor for thirteen years. The Habsburgs are consolidating their grip on the imperial crown; their marital diplomacy will soon assemble an empire reaching from Spain to Hungary.

polities.name: Kingdom of Castile
polities.desc: Isabella, future co-ruler with Ferdinand of Aragon, is two years old. The Reconquista has thirty-nine years left to run. Columbus is an unknown Genoese boy.

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.desc: Portuguese caravels have begun exploring the West African coast under Prince Henry the Navigator. The systematic search for a sea route to India is underway — it will reach fruition with Vasco da Gama in 1498.

polities.name: Ming China
polities.desc: The Jingtai Emperor reigns after the Tumu crisis. Zheng He's last voyage was twenty years ago; the Treasure Fleet has been dismantled. China is consolidating inward just as Europe begins reaching outward. At this moment the dynasty controls 'China proper' — the eighteen historical provinces south of the Great Wall.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
polities.desc: Vasili II rules. In twenty-seven years his son Ivan III will end the Mongol tribute and begin Moscow's rise to empire. The doctrine of Moscow as the 'Third Rome' is taking shape. At this moment Muscovy is a modest principality in central European Russia — the annexation of Novgorod is a generation away.

polities.name: Mamluk Sultanate
polities.desc: The Burji dynasty rules Egypt, Syria, and the Hejaz. Still the principal Arab power, but increasingly overshadowed by the rising Ottomans. Selim I will conquer them in 1517.

polities.name: Sultanate of Delhi (Lodi)
polities.desc: The Lodi Afghans have just seized power. The sultanate controls only the upper Indo-Gangetic plain; much of the subcontinent is under independent sultans or Hindu kingdoms.

polities.name: Songhai Empire
polities.desc: West African empire on the Niger, just beginning its rise under Sunni Ali. Will dominate the trans-Saharan trade and inherit Mali's mantle as the region's great power.

polities.name: Aztec Triple Alliance
polities.desc: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan dominates central Mexico. Moctezuma I has just expanded the empire eastward to the Gulf coast.

polities.name: Inca Empire
polities.desc: Pachacuti has built the Andean empire from a minor Cusco state into a civilization spanning thousands of miles. The imperial road system and terraced agriculture date from this period.

name: Reformation
desc: Luther posts the Ninety-Five Theses at Wittenberg. Within a generation Latin Christendom will be permanently split. The religious wars that follow will kill millions and, by exhausting everyone, produce the modern state system.

events.name: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses
events.desc: On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther posts (or sends) his ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences at the Castle Church in Wittenberg. The printing press turns a local academic complaint into a pan-European movement within months.

events.name: Conquest of the Aztec Empire
events.desc: After a 75-day siege, Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies take Tenochtitlan. The Aztec Empire, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, falls to perhaps 1,000 Spaniards and 100,000 Indigenous troops. Smallpox arrives with the invaders and kills tens of millions over the following century.

events.name: Magellan's Circumnavigation
events.desc: Magellan is killed in the Philippines in 1521; Elcano brings the Victoria home to Spain in 1522 with 18 survivors from the original 270. The first circumnavigation of the globe establishes empirically that the oceans of the world are connected and the earth is round.

events.name: Publication of The Prince
events.desc: Niccolò Machiavelli writes *Il Principe* in Florence, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici. The first modern treatise on politics as craft rather than moral philosophy. Banned by the Church; indispensable to every subsequent political thinker.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.desc: Charles V rules — king of Spain, Holy Roman Emperor, ruler of the Netherlands, Naples, and the Spanish colonies in the Americas. The closest any power has come to universal monarchy in Europe since Rome. Luther's challenge will fracture his empire religiously even as external wars strain it militarily.
polities.note: Rendered here as a single unit per the historical moment — the HRE in 1517 still functioned as a real political entity before the Reformation shattered it.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.desc: Francis I rules. France is the perennial rival of the Habsburgs, hemmed in on every land border. Will spend the next century fighting to break the encirclement.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.desc: Henry VIII is nine years into his reign. Still a Catholic king; still married to Catherine of Aragon. The break with Rome is fifteen years away.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Selim the Grim has just conquered Egypt and claimed the caliphate. Suleiman the Magnificent will take the throne in 1520 and drive Ottoman power to its historical peak. The Christian states of Europe are terrified.
polities.note: The Ottoman threat from the east is the constant background pressure that shapes every other European calculation in this century.

polities.name: Safavid Persia
polities.desc: Shah Ismail's new Shia dynasty, established in 1501. The Ottoman–Safavid rivalry is the defining conflict of the Islamic world for the next two centuries and cements the Sunni–Shia sectarian line.

polities.name: Mughal Precursors
polities.desc: Babur is consolidating control in Kabul. In nine years he will cross the Khyber, defeat the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat, and found the Mughal Empire.

polities.name: Delhi Sultanate (terminal)
polities.desc: The Lodi dynasty rules a much-diminished sultanate. Ibrahim Lodi will die at Panipat in 1526 and the dynasty with him.

polities.name: Ming China
polities.desc: The Zhengde Emperor reigns. A century after Zheng He's voyages, China has turned decisively inward. A vast, wealthy, self-sufficient civilization choosing isolation from the wider world. The dynasty controls 'China proper' — the eighteen historical provinces south of the Great Wall.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
polities.desc: Vasili III rules. The Mongol yoke was broken only forty years ago. Ivan the Terrible, who will declare himself tsar, is Vasili's unborn son. Muscovy has annexed Novgorod (1478), Tver (1485), and Pskov (1510), but Siberia and the Volga steppe are still beyond its reach.

polities.name: Aztec Empire
polities.desc: Moctezuma II rules. Cortés will land in two years and the empire will not survive the decade. Tenochtitlan at this moment is larger than any city in Europe.

polities.name: Inca Empire
polities.desc: Huayna Capac rules. The empire is at its territorial peak, running from modern Colombia to Chile. Smallpox, arriving ahead of the Spanish, will kill Huayna Capac and trigger the civil war that Pizarro will exploit.

name: Westphalian Settlement
desc: The Thirty Years' War ends. The treaty system codifies state sovereignty as the operating principle of European politics. The world order our diplomats still inhabit begins here.

events.name: Peace of Westphalia
events.desc: Signed at Münster and Osnabrück, ending the Thirty Years' War (8 million dead) and the Eighty Years' War. Establishes the principles of state sovereignty and non-interference that still formally structure international relations.

events.name: English Civil War: Execution of Charles I
events.desc: Charles I is beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. The first European monarch executed by his own people on constitutional grounds. The Commonwealth period follows — England's republican experiment.

events.name: Construction of the Taj Mahal
events.desc: Shah Jahan completes the Taj Mahal at Agra as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. The project took 22 years and 20,000 workers. The Mughal Empire is at its cultural peak just as its fiscal foundations are beginning to erode.

events.name: Portuguese settle Macau
events.desc: 1557. Portuguese traders, already working the Canton coast for two decades, secure informal Ming permission to establish a permanent trading post on a small peninsula at the mouth of the Pearl River in exchange for suppressing local piracy. Macau becomes the first European settlement in China and the hinge of the silver-for-silk trade: Spanish silver from Potosí and Japanese silver from Iwami flow through Macau in exchange for Chinese silk, porcelain, and tea. Jesuit missionaries — Matteo Ricci, Adam Schall — use the city as their entry into the Ming court. Macau remains Portuguese for 442 years, the longest-held European possession in Asia, returned to China only in 1999.

polities.name: Spanish Empire
polities.desc: The first global empire on which the sun never set. Silver from Potosí financed European wars and inflated prices across three continents.
polities.note: The original blueprint for transoceanic empire — and the first to demonstrate how extractive wealth corrodes the metropole.

polities.name: Portuguese Empire
polities.desc: Independence from the Iberian Union restored in 1640 under João IV. By 1648 Portugal is fighting the Restoration War against Spain while consolidating a global trading empire built on fortified coastal enclaves rather than territorial conquest.
polities.note: The first pattern of European seaborne empire — the fortress-and-factory model that the Dutch and English would later scale up into something far larger.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.desc: Louis XIV is ten years old. Cardinal Mazarin governs. The Fronde is brewing. Within a generation France will dominate Europe.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire (post-Westphalia)
polities.desc: Effectively dissolved as a real political entity by the 1648 settlement. Some 300 sovereign units now bound only by ceremony.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Past its high-water mark at Vienna's gates but still controlling the eastern Mediterranean, North Africa, and the Balkans. The principal Muslim power.

polities.name: Mughal Empire
polities.desc: Shah Jahan rules. The Taj Mahal is being built. Mughal India produces perhaps a quarter of global GDP.

polities.name: Qing China (early)
polities.desc: The Manchus have just conquered Beijing. The conquest of Ming loyalist territories in the south will continue for decades.

polities.name: Tsardom of Russia
polities.desc: Alexis I rules. Cossack expansion across Siberia is in full swing. The state is recovering from the Time of Troubles.

name: The Company Era
desc: The Battle of Plassey. The East India Company, a private joint-stock corporation chartered in London in 1600, becomes the effective sovereign of Bengal. For the next century, chartered companies — not kingdoms — administer a meaningful share of the planet. This map shows the companies themselves as the polities.

events.name: Battle of Plassey
events.desc: Robert Clive, with 3,000 EIC troops and a secret agreement with the Bengali commander Mir Jafar, defeats Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah's 50,000-strong army. The company installs Mir Jafar as puppet ruler and takes de facto control of Bengal's revenue. The richest province in the subcontinent becomes a corporate asset.

events.name: Capture of Quebec
events.desc: British forces under Wolfe defeat the French on the Plains of Abraham. Both commanders die. The Seven Years' War (the true first world war — fought on five continents) ends French colonial power in North America and establishes Britain as the dominant global empire.

events.name: Lisbon Earthquake
events.desc: On All Saints' Day, a magnitude-8.5 earthquake, tsunami, and fire destroy Lisbon. Perhaps 60,000 dead. The catastrophe reshapes European theodicy — Voltaire's *Candide* is a direct response — and accelerates Enlightenment skepticism about providential design.

polities.name: East India Company
polities.desc: Founded 1600. Maintains its own army (260,000 men by 1803), its own navy, mints its own currency, collects its own taxes. By 1803 the Company will govern 90 million people in the subcontinent — roughly the population of France and Britain combined.
polities.note: The Company's sovereign powers over its territories were not fully revoked by the British Crown until 1858, after the Sepoy Mutiny. For 250 years, private capital held the powers of a state.

polities.name: British North America
polities.desc: The Thirteen Colonies plus the Maritime provinces (Nova Scotia acquired 1713, Newfoundland 1713) and the Caribbean sugar islands. Administered under royal charters, proprietary grants, and the Navigation Acts. The frictions between colonial assemblies and the imperial center will produce rebellion within two decades.
polities.note: Not a chartered company itself, but the colonial order that the Company Era's trading networks depended on for New World silver, sugar, tobacco, and naval stores.

polities.name: Dutch East India Company (VOC)
polities.desc: Founded 1602. The first multinational corporation and the first to issue stock. Ruled Indonesia, Taiwan (until 1662), Cape Colony, and the Spice Islands. By 1669 owned 150 merchant ships and 40 warships; employed 50,000 men. Bankrupt in 1799 and nationalized by the Dutch state.

polities.name: Hudson's Bay Company
polities.desc: Founded 1670. Granted monopoly trading rights over Rupert's Land — the entire Hudson Bay watershed, roughly 40 percent of modern Canada. Governed the territory directly, operating as a de facto sovereign, until 1870.

polities.name: New France
polities.desc: The French colonial empire in North America — the St. Lawrence valley, the Great Lakes, and Louisiana. Will be lost to Britain in the Seven Years' War (Quebec falls 1759, Montreal 1760, formalized at Paris 1763). At 1757 still intact but militarily outmatched.

polities.name: French Compagnie des Indes
polities.desc: Colbert's 1664 reorganization of earlier French trading companies. Rival to the EIC in India; held Pondicherry, Chandernagore, and posts in Africa and the Caribbean. Will be broken by the EIC in the Carnatic Wars and absorbed by the French state in 1769.

polities.name: Royal African Company
polities.desc: Chartered 1672. Held an English monopoly on the West African slave trade until 1698. Administered forts on the Gold Coast and Gambia. The primary legal vehicle for English participation in the Atlantic slave trade during its peak decades.
polities.note: Joint-stock imperialism meant that the institutional apparatus of early modern slavery was corporate, not royal. Shareholders included the Royal Society, Samuel Pepys, and John Locke.

polities.name: Russian-American Company
polities.desc: The Russian Pacific enterprise begins with Vitus Bering's 1741 expedition and is consolidated by Grigory Shelekhov's Three Saints Bay settlement in 1784. Paul I will charter the monopoly Russian-American Company in 1799, which administers Alaska, the Aleutians, Kamchatka, and the Kuril Islands from Sitka. Sea-otter fur is the commodity; Fort Ross in California (1812) marks the southern edge of Russian America. Alaska will be sold to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million — 'Seward's Folly' that turns out to contain oil and gold.

polities.name: Spanish Empire
polities.desc: Ferdinand VI rules an empire that still dwarfs every European rival in territorial extent. The Viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru supply the silver that underwrites Habsburg and Bourbon Europe alike. The Philippines govern from Manila under Spanish authority. The Bourbon Reforms are rationalizing the administration, but the empire will be shaken by the Seven Years' War — Havana and Manila briefly fall to Britain in 1762.
polities.note: The Spanish Empire governed roughly 13 million people in the Americas at this point — more than Britain's North American colonies and India combined — and would remain the world's largest silver producer until Mexican independence in 1821.

polities.name: Qing China
polities.desc: The Qianlong Emperor's reign is at its peak — the largest, wealthiest, and most populous empire on earth. The Canton System restricts European trade to a single port, a policy the British East India Company will break by force in the 1840s.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Mustafa III reigns over an empire that still stretches from Algeria to the Persian Gulf but is increasingly dependent on European powers for technical and military modernization.

polities.name: Mughal Empire (collapsing)
polities.desc: Shah Alam II is Emperor in name. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739; Ahmad Shah Durrani has done it again in 1757. The real powers in the subcontinent are the Marathas, the EIC, and regional successor states.

polities.name: Maratha Confederacy
polities.desc: The dominant Indian power of the 18th century. A loose confederacy of chieftains controlling most of central and western India. Will be defeated decisively by Ahmad Shah Durrani at Panipat in 1761, creating the power vacuum the EIC exploits.

name: American Revolution
desc: Thirteen British colonies declare independence. The republic they establish will become the dominant great power of the twentieth century and export its founding ideology to every continent. The Enlightenment becomes a territorial state.

events.name: Declaration of Independence
events.desc: The Second Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence at Independence Hall in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776. Jefferson's draft, revised by Franklin and Adams, is the first government document to ground legitimacy explicitly in natural rights theory.

events.name: Publication of *The Wealth of Nations*
events.desc: Adam Smith publishes *An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations* in Edinburgh. The foundational text of modern economics. Smith is sharply critical of chartered monopolies like the East India Company — which will be reformed within a decade partly in response.

events.name: Battle of Yorktown
events.desc: Washington and Rochambeau trap Cornwallis on the Yorktown peninsula. The French fleet blocks escape. After a three-week siege Cornwallis surrenders 7,000 troops. The British government falls; peace negotiations begin.

events.name: Storming of the Bastille
events.desc: A Parisian crowd takes the Bastille fortress in search of gunpowder. The event marks the start of the French Revolution. Within a decade France will abolish feudalism, execute its king, invent modern nationalism, and begin a quarter-century of war that reshapes Europe.

events.name: First Fleet to Botany Bay
events.desc: The British First Fleet arrives at Sydney Cove with 780 convicts and their guards, establishing the colony of New South Wales. Transportation is partly a response to the American Revolution cutting off the previous convict destination.

polities.name: United States (nascent)
polities.desc: The Continental Congress has just issued the Declaration. The war will run another seven years. The Constitution is eleven years away. A republic of four million people, mostly east of the Appalachians — a narrow coastal strip of what will become the modern United States.
polities.note: The first modern revolutionary state, and the first since antiquity to be founded on an explicit theory of natural rights rather than dynastic inheritance or conquest.

polities.name: British Empire (first)
polities.desc: George III rules. Britain is losing the Americas but gaining India — Clive's victories in Bengal have made the East India Company the effective ruler of the subcontinent. The 'First British Empire' ends here; the 'Second,' centered on Asia, is just beginning. After the Seven Years' War, Britain's Canadian holdings are the former New France (Province of Quebec after 1763) plus the Maritime provinces. Rupert's Land — the Hudson Bay watershed — is governed separately by the Hudson's Bay Company under royal charter.

polities.name: Hudson's Bay Company (Rupert's Land)
polities.desc: Chartered 1670. In 1776 it governs the Hudson Bay watershed — roughly 40 percent of modern Canada — as a de facto sovereign entity. The charter will be transferred to the Canadian government in 1870. Pacific slope (modern British Columbia and Yukon) is not British at all in 1776.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.desc: Louis XVI reigns. France will fund the American rebels to weaken Britain — and bankrupt itself doing so. The financial crisis will produce the Estates-General, then the Revolution, then Napoleon. A line traces straight from Yorktown to the guillotine.

polities.name: Spanish Empire
polities.desc: Charles III is the last great Bourbon reformer. The empire still spans from California to Cape Horn, but the Bourbon reforms are generating as much colonial resentment as revenue. Independence movements will come within a generation.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire (twilight)
polities.desc: Joseph II is Holy Roman Emperor. The empire is a shell; Prussia and Austria are the real German powers. Napoleon will formally dissolve it in thirty years.

polities.name: Russian Empire
polities.desc: Catherine the Great rules. Russia is expanding against the Ottomans in the south and partitioning Poland in the west. Pugachev's revolt has just been crushed.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Abdul Hamid I reigns. Losing ground steadily to Russia and Austria. The century of decline is well underway.

polities.name: Qing China
polities.desc: The Qianlong Emperor's reign is near its peak. China is by most measures the world's largest economy and the dominant Asian power. Within a century the opium wars will shatter this self-image.

polities.name: Mughal Empire (vestigial)
polities.desc: Shah Alam II is a Mughal emperor in name only. Real power in the subcontinent is now divided between the Marathas, the East India Company, and regional successor states.

name: Napoleonic Apogee
desc: The Grand Army crosses the Niemen into Russia. Napoleon rules directly or through client states from Madrid to Warsaw — the largest territorial consolidation Europe has seen since Charlemagne. By winter his army will be destroyed.

events.name: Battle of Borodino
events.desc: The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars — 70,000 combined casualties in twelve hours. A tactical French victory that lets Napoleon take Moscow, but strategically indecisive. Moscow burns; the Russian army remains in the field; the disaster of the winter retreat follows.

events.name: Burning of Moscow
events.desc: Russian forces set Moscow ablaze rather than leave it intact for French occupation. Three-quarters of the city burns over four days. Napoleon occupies the ruins for five weeks waiting for a tsar's surrender that never comes, then begins the catastrophic retreat.

events.name: Battle of Waterloo
events.desc: Wellington and Blücher defeat Napoleon's final bid for power after his return from Elba. The end of the Napoleonic era. The Congress of Vienna settles Europe's borders for the next forty years and invents the concert-of-powers diplomacy that will hold until 1914.

events.name: Start of Latin American Independence
events.desc: The Cry of Independence in Bogotá in 1810 and the Grito de Dolores in Mexico in the same year begin the collapse of Spanish America. Within fifteen years, Bolívar and San Martín will have ended three centuries of Spanish rule on the continent.

events.name: Louisiana Purchase
events.desc: Napoleon sells 828,000 square miles — the entire Mississippi watershed from New Orleans to the Rockies — to Jefferson's United States for $15 million, about 3 cents an acre. France, having reacquired the territory from Spain in 1800, needs cash for the coming European war and cannot defend it after losing Saint-Domingue (Haiti) to the Haitian Revolution. The single stroke doubles US territory, eliminates a European rival from mid-continent, and opens the path to Pacific expansion.

events.name: Lewis and Clark Expedition
events.desc: The Corps of Discovery reaches the Pacific near the mouth of the Columbia River after a two-and-a-half-year overland journey from St. Louis. Their maps, specimens, and diplomatic contacts with Native nations lay the factual basis for American claims to the continent's western half.

polities.name: First French Empire
polities.desc: Napoleon's empire at its territorial maximum. The Rhine Confederation, the Duchy of Warsaw, the Kingdom of Italy, the Kingdom of Naples, and occupied Spain are all effectively extensions of French power. The Code Napoléon is being imposed across Europe.
polities.note: The only sustained attempt since Rome to unify Europe by force — and the template for the two later attempts that followed in the twentieth century.

polities.name: Russian Empire
polities.desc: Alexander I trades space for time. Moscow will burn in September. The Grand Army will die in the retreat. Russia will emerge from 1815 as the greatest land power in Europe. Across the Pacific, the Russian-American Company (chartered 1799) administers Russian Alaska from New Archangel (Sitka); Fort Ross is founded in California in 1812 as its southern fur-trade outpost. Alaska will remain Russian until sold to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million.

polities.name: British Empire
polities.desc: The Royal Navy dominates the oceans. The Peninsular War in Spain ties down French forces. Britain is financing the coalition that will ultimately destroy Napoleon. British North America stretches from Upper Canada to Newfoundland; the Hudson's Bay Company still governs Rupert's Land. In Asia, the East India Company controls most of the subcontinent.

polities.name: Hudson's Bay Company (Rupert's Land)
polities.desc: HBC still governs the Hudson Bay watershed. The fur-trade war with the rival North West Company is in full swing and will end in forced merger in 1821.

polities.name: Austrian Empire
polities.desc: Emperor Francis I has transformed the Habsburg domains into the Austrian Empire after Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. A reluctant French ally in 1812; will defect in 1813.

polities.name: Kingdom of Prussia
polities.desc: Crushed by Napoleon at Jena in 1806 and reduced to a French satellite. The humiliation is driving the military and administrative reforms that will make Prussia the core of a unified Germany by 1871.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Mahmud II rules. The Serbian uprising is underway. The Greek revolt will begin in nine years. The long unraveling of the empire into nation-states is visible in outline.

polities.name: United States
polities.desc: James Madison has just declared war on Britain. The War of 1812 will go badly — the White House will burn in 1814 — but the republic will survive and confirm its independence. Eighteen states by April 1812 (Louisiana being the newest), with the Louisiana Purchase and the Northwest, Indiana, and Mississippi Territories extending federal sovereignty to the Rockies.

polities.name: Spanish America (in revolt)
polities.desc: With Spain under French occupation, the colonies have begun their independence wars. Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín are launching the campaigns that will end Spanish rule on the continent within fifteen years.

polities.name: Qing China
polities.desc: The Jiaqing Emperor reigns. The White Lotus Rebellion has drained the treasury. The dynasty is entering its long structural decline; the First Opium War is twenty-seven years away. The empire still encompasses China proper, Manchuria, Mongolia, Xinjiang, and Tibet — roughly the modern Chinese borders plus outer Mongolia.

polities.name: British India (Company Raj)
polities.desc: The East India Company governs most of the subcontinent. The Marathas have been defeated; the remaining princely states are clients. The Crown will not take over until 1858.

name: American Civil War
desc: Gettysburg and Vicksburg. The existential crisis of the American republic. The war will decide whether the United States remains a slaveholding confederation or becomes a continental industrial nation — and the answer will shape the twentieth century.

events.name: Battle of Gettysburg
events.desc: July 1–3, 1863. Lee's invasion of the North is broken on the third day with Pickett's Charge across open ground into Union artillery. 51,000 combined casualties — more than any battle in American history. The Confederacy will never again mount a strategic offensive.

events.name: Siege of Vicksburg
events.desc: Grant takes Vicksburg on July 4 after a forty-seven-day siege. The Union now controls the entire Mississippi River. The Confederacy is cut in half. The twin victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in the same week are the war's strategic turning point.

events.name: Fort Sumter
events.desc: Confederate forces bombard the Union-held Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. The garrison surrenders the next day. The war begins. Four years and 750,000 American dead later, slavery is abolished and the federal government has definitively subordinated the states.

events.name: Emancipation Proclamation
events.desc: Effective January 1, 1863. Lincoln declares slaves in Confederate territory 'forever free.' The proclamation has no immediate practical force — it applies only where the US has no control — but it transforms the war's purpose and blocks any possible European recognition of the Confederacy.

events.name: Opening of Japan (Meiji Restoration begins)
events.desc: The Meiji Restoration transfers power from the Tokugawa shogunate to Emperor Meiji. Over the next thirty years Japan will build railways, a modern army and navy, universal education, and heavy industry. The first non-Western state to industrialize.

events.name: Drake's Well
events.desc: Edwin Drake drills the first commercially successful oil well in Titusville, Pennsylvania. 69 feet down, 25 barrels a day. The rock-oil industry is born — initially for kerosene lamps replacing whale oil. The true age of hydrocarbons begins.

events.name: Standard Oil founded
events.desc: John D. Rockefeller, aged 31, incorporates Standard Oil of Ohio. By 1882 he controls 90 percent of American refining through the trust form he invents. Broken up in 1911 but its descendants — Exxon, Chevron, BP via Anglo-American — remain at the center of the hydrocarbon economy.

events.name: Raffles founds Singapore
events.desc: January 29, 1819. Stamford Raffles of the East India Company lands on a swampy island of about a thousand Malays and Chinese fishermen at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Within a week he has signed a treaty with the Temenggong and the Sultan of Johor granting a British trading post. Declared a free port, Singapore's population reaches 10,000 within five years and 80,000 by 1860. The choke point of the Strait of Malacca — the shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and China — is now in British hands. Within a century Singapore is the busiest port in Asia; within two, the wealthiest city in Southeast Asia and the model developmental state of the post-colonial era.

events.name: Treaty of Nanking — Hong Kong ceded
events.desc: August 29, 1842. After three years of the First Opium War — British gunboats up the Yangtze and Grand Canal, the Qing humiliated at every engagement — China cedes Hong Kong Island 'in perpetuity' to Queen Victoria, opens five treaty ports (Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, Shanghai) to British residence and trade, abolishes the Cohong monopoly, and pays a $21 million indemnity. The first of the 'unequal treaties.' Kowloon is added in 1860; the New Territories leased for 99 years in 1898. Hong Kong grows from a rocky fishing anchorage into one of the world's great entrepôts — refuge from every upheaval on the mainland, financial hinge between China and the Western world.

events.name: Suez Canal opens
events.desc: November 17, 1869. After ten years of construction under Ferdinand de Lesseps and a Franco-Egyptian company — with perhaps 120,000 Egyptian laborers dead in the cutting — a 164-kilometer channel connects the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The voyage from London to Bombay is cut from 20,000 to 12,000 kilometers. Egypt's ruler Ismail Pasha opens the canal in a ceremony featuring Verdi's commission for Aida. Within six years Egypt is bankrupt; Britain's Disraeli borrows from the Rothschilds overnight to buy the Khedive's 44 percent stake. British occupation of Egypt follows in 1882 and lasts seventy years; the canal becomes the single most strategically important choke point of the imperial era, fought over at El Alamein in 1942 and nationalized by Nasser in 1956.

polities.name: Union (United States)
polities.desc: Lincoln's government. Twenty million people, industrial base, naval superiority. The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1st. The summer of 1863 marks the war's turning point.
polities.note: The Union's victory cemented the political unification of the North American continent under a single industrial power — the necessary precondition for everything the United States became in the following century.

polities.name: Confederate States
polities.desc: Jefferson Davis presides over eleven seceded states and nine million people, four million of them enslaved. Cotton exports were supposed to force British recognition; they have not. The war has two more years.

polities.name: US Territories (unorganized & frontier)
polities.desc: The trans-Mississippi West — Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Washington territories. Legally Union but administered separately, with only scattered non-Native populations. Indian Territory (modern Oklahoma) is claimed by both sides and contains its own small civil war among the Five Tribes.

polities.name: British Empire
polities.desc: Palmerston governs. The Crown has taken direct control of India from the East India Company five years ago. The cotton famine from the Union blockade is wrecking Lancashire, but Britain stays neutral.

polities.name: French Empire
polities.desc: Napoleon III rules. French troops are installing Maximilian as Emperor of Mexico right now — a direct challenge to the Monroe Doctrine that will collapse once the Civil War ends and the US can enforce it.

polities.name: Russian Empire
polities.desc: Alexander II freed the serfs two years ago. Russia diplomatically supports the Union against Britain and France. The Russian fleet will visit New York and San Francisco this autumn as a gesture of solidarity.

polities.name: Austrian Empire
polities.desc: Franz Joseph reigns over a multinational empire. Three years after defeat in the Second Italian War, facing a Prussian challenge within three more. The Ausgleich creating Austria-Hungary is four years away.

polities.name: Kingdom of Prussia
polities.desc: Bismarck has just become Minister-President. The wars that will unify Germany — against Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870 — are imminent.

polities.name: Kingdom of Italy
polities.desc: Italy was unified only two years ago under Victor Emmanuel II. Rome is still papal; Venice is still Austrian. Both will be acquired within a decade.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.desc: Abdülaziz reigns over the Tanzimat reforms. The empire is attempting constitutional and economic modernization. The Crimean War and its financial aftermath have compromised sovereignty to European creditors.

polities.name: Qing China
polities.desc: The Taiping Rebellion is in its final year — perhaps twenty million dead. The Second Opium War ended three years ago; Beijing was occupied; the Summer Palace burned. The dynasty has entered terminal decline.

polities.name: Empire of Japan (pre-Meiji)
polities.desc: The Tokugawa shogunate is unraveling under Western pressure. The Meiji Restoration is five years away. Japan will emerge from it as the first non-Western industrial power.

polities.name: Mexican Empire (Second)
polities.desc: French troops took Mexico City in June. Maximilian of Austria will arrive next year as Emperor. The Juárez republican government is fighting from the north. The empire will collapse in 1867.

polities.name: Empire of Brazil
polities.desc: Pedro II reigns over the only constitutional monarchy in the Americas. Brazil is at war with Paraguay from 1864. Slavery persists; will not be abolished until 1888.
