polities.name: New Caledonia (French)
polities.desc: Annexed by France in 1853.

name: Age of Empires
desc: The European empires have partitioned Africa and most of Asia. The British Empire covers a quarter of the earth's land surface. The United States has just become a Pacific power.

events.name: Boxer Rebellion
events.desc: The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists besieges the foreign legations in Beijing. An eight-nation alliance — Britain, the US, Germany, France, Russia, Japan, Italy, Austria-Hungary — lifts the siege, imposes a crushing indemnity, and makes the Qing dynasty's collapse inevitable.

events.name: Battle of Omdurman
events.desc: Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army annihilates the Mahdist forces outside Khartoum. 11,000 Sudanese dead to 48 British. Winston Churchill, there as a young lieutenant, called it 'the most signal triumph ever gained by the arms of science over barbarians.' The maxim gun had its first major field test.

events.name: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.desc: Orville Wright flies a powered aircraft for twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Within sixty-five years humans will land on the moon.

events.name: Spanish-American War
events.desc: The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor triggers a war that ends Spain's empire. The United States emerges with Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines — its first overseas colonies. Imperial in fact, republican in self-image.

events.name: Baku Oil Boom
events.desc: At the turn of the century the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian produces roughly half the world's oil. The Nobel brothers (Ludvig, Robert, and Alfred of prize fame) and the Rothschilds build the first integrated oil industry — pipelines, tankers, refineries. Baku's oil wealth funds the Russian industrial revolution and, via Bolshevik organizer Joseph Stalin's early career there, the revolution that will overthrow it. The city is the first Los Angeles, the first Houston — a raw, multiethnic boomtown of Armenians, Azeris, Russians, Persians, and European capital.

events.name: Standard Oil Broken Up
events.desc: The Supreme Court orders the dissolution of John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil under the Sherman Antitrust Act. At its peak Standard controls 90 percent of American refining and much of world kerosene distribution. The breakup creates 34 companies, the ancestors of ExxonMobil, Chevron, Amoco, Marathon, and the rest of the modern oil majors. Rockefeller becomes the richest man in modern history. The case sets the template for 20th-century antitrust — and will be invoked a century later against the tech giants.

events.name: Anglo-Persian Oil Concession
events.desc: William Knox D'Arcy's wildcatters strike oil at Masjed Soleyman in southwest Persia — the first commercial oil discovery in the Middle East. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (today BP) is founded the following year. In 1914 Winston Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, persuades Parliament to buy a majority stake and convert the Royal Navy from coal to oil. The move ties British strategy to Persian Gulf security for the rest of the century and invents the politics of the modern Middle East.

events.name: Baku oil boom
events.desc: Branobel (the Nobel brothers' company) and the Rothschilds' Caspian and Black Sea Company turn Baku into the source of roughly half the world's oil. Russian, Swedish, French, and American capital flows into a frontier city on the Caspian. The Nobel Prize is partly funded by Baku crude.

events.name: Spindletop gusher
events.desc: January 10, 1901. A well on Spindletop Hill near Beaumont, Texas blows in at 100,000 barrels a day — more than all other US wells combined. Texaco and Gulf Oil are founded to exploit the find. American oil's center of gravity moves from Pennsylvania to the Gulf coast.

events.name: Anglo-Persian Oil
events.desc: William Knox D'Arcy's concession strikes oil at Masjed Soleyman in Persia. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (later BP) is founded in 1909. Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, converts the Royal Navy from coal to oil and takes the British government as majority shareholder — making Middle Eastern oil a British strategic interest for the next fifty years.

events.name: Drake's Well — birth of the oil industry
events.desc: Edwin Drake drills the first commercially successful oil well near Titusville, Pennsylvania, at 69 feet using a steam-powered rig. Within a year a forest of derricks covers Oil Creek Valley; Pithole City goes from farmland to 15,000 people in eighteen months. Kerosene for lighting displaces whale oil within a decade, saving the whales by accident. John D. Rockefeller arrives in 1863. The modern petroleum industry — and every politics that follows from it — begins here.

events.name: Transcontinental Railroad completed
events.desc: The Central Pacific and Union Pacific meet at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. Leland Stanford drives the golden spike. A journey that took six months by wagon now takes a week. The railroad is built largely by Chinese and Irish labor; it accelerates the closing of the frontier, the destruction of the Plains buffalo, and the subjugation of the Plains nations. The continental United States becomes, for the first time, a single market.

events.name: Panama Canal opens
events.desc: After a French attempt that killed 22,000 workers to yellow fever and malaria, the United States completes the canal in ten years. 77 kilometers of locks and artificial lakes cut the voyage from New York to San Francisco by 13,000 kilometers. The canal formalizes American hemispheric dominance — the Panama Canal Zone is US territory until 1999 — and reorders global shipping. The Roosevelt Corollary, dollar diplomacy, and a century of US Caribbean interventions flow from its strategic logic.

polities.name: British Empire
polities.desc: The largest empire in history by area. India is the jewel; the dominions of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa are self-governing; Africa is being consolidated.
polities.note: Pax Britannica was the second great thalassocracy. The naval logic of Athens and Rome, scaled to the planet.

polities.name: French Colonial Empire
polities.desc: Algeria, Indochina, West Africa. The second largest colonial empire, often presented as a 'mission civilisatrice' — a civilizing mission.

polities.name: Russian Empire
polities.desc: Nicholas II rules a vast multinational empire from Poland to Vladivostok. The Trans-Siberian Railway is nearly complete. Revolutionary pressure is building.

polities.name: German Empire
polities.desc: Wilhelm II reigns. The fastest-growing industrial economy in Europe. A naval program is underway that will alarm Britain into the Triple Entente.

polities.name: Austria-Hungary
polities.desc: The multinational Habsburg empire. Twelve major nationalities, three official languages, and increasing internal pressure.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire (declining)
polities.desc: The 'sick man of Europe.' Reduced to Anatolia, the Levant, and parts of Arabia. Will not survive the coming war.

polities.name: Qing China (terminal)
polities.desc: The dynasty has barely a decade left. Foreign concessions, the Boxer Rebellion, and the humiliation of the unequal treaties have hollowed out central authority.

polities.name: United States
polities.desc: Just emerged from the Spanish-American War with the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico. McKinley is president. Imperial in fact, republican in self-image.

polities.name: Empire of Japan
polities.desc: Meiji modernization complete. Just defeated Qing China in 1895. Will defeat Russia in 1905. The first non-Western great power of the modern era.

polities.name: Kingdom of Italy
polities.desc: Umberto I is assassinated by an anarchist at Monza in July 1900; Victor Emmanuel III succeeds him. A newly unified country — the Risorgimento ended only in 1870 — grappling with the 'Southern Question,' mass emigration to the Americas, and late-arriving colonial ambitions. The humiliation at Adwa in 1896 (Ethiopia the only African state to defeat a European army) still stings; Libya lies ahead in 1911.

polities.name: Kingdom of Spain
polities.desc: Alfonso XIII is a minor on the throne. The disaster of 1898 — Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam lost to the United States — has ended four centuries of Spanish empire in the Americas and Pacific. What remains is Spanish Morocco, the Sahara, Equatorial Guinea, and a wounded national self-image that will fuel the Generation of '98 and, eventually, civil war.

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.desc: Carlos I reigns over the oldest European colonial empire: Angola, Mozambique, Portuguese Guinea, Cape Verde, São Tomé, Goa, Macau, and East Timor. The monarchy has ten years left — Carlos will be assassinated in 1908, the republic proclaimed in 1910.

polities.name: Netherlands & Dutch East Indies
polities.desc: Wilhelmina rules the Netherlands and, through the Royal Dutch East Indies Army, 70 million Indonesians across Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, and the Moluccas. Royal Dutch Petroleum (1890) and Shell Transport (1897) are in the process of merging; the profits of Sumatran oil and Javanese sugar make Amsterdam one of the wealthiest cities in Europe. The Aceh War drags into its thirtieth year.

polities.name: Belgium & Congo Free State
polities.desc: Leopold II's personal colonial property — the Congo Free State — is a slave-labor rubber regime the size of western Europe. Between 1885 and 1908 perhaps ten million Congolese die from violence, famine, and disease. Roger Casement's 1904 report and E.D. Morel's Congo Reform Association will force the state's transfer to the Belgian government in 1908.

polities.name: Scandinavian Kingdoms
polities.desc: Sweden and Norway remain in personal union under Oscar II — the union will dissolve peacefully in 1905. Denmark under Christian IX is Europe's 'grandfather-in-law,' with daughters on the British and Russian thrones. Iceland is still a Danish dependency. The region's industrial, social-democratic trajectory is visible.

polities.name: Swiss Confederation
polities.desc: The only large European republic. Armed neutrality; direct democracy via referendum since 1848. The Red Cross (1863), the headquarters of the Universal Postal Union and Berne Convention, and a quiet emerging role as the banking center of continental Europe.

polities.name: Kingdom of Greece & the Balkans
polities.desc: The new states carved out of the Ottoman retreat: Greece (independent 1830), Serbia and Romania (1878), Bulgaria (1878 autonomous, 1908 fully independent), Montenegro (1878). All nurture irredentist claims on Ottoman Macedonia and Thrace. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by Serbian nationalists in 1914 is fourteen years away.

polities.name: Siam (independent)
polities.desc: Chulalongkorn's reign. The only Southeast Asian kingdom to avoid colonization, by skillful diplomacy between British Burma and French Indochina and an aggressive program of modernization — railways, telegraphs, Western-style ministries, the abolition of slavery.

polities.name: Persia (Qajar)
polities.desc: Mozaffar ad-Din Shah's weakened Qajar state. Anglo-Russian rivalry carves spheres of influence; the Constitutional Revolution of 1906 is six years away. The D'Arcy oil concession of 1901 will transform the country's strategic weight.

polities.name: Ethiopian Empire
polities.desc: Menelik II has just defeated the Italians at Adwa (1896), the only African state to survive the Scramble with its independence intact. A Christian polity older than most European states, claiming descent from Solomon.

polities.name: Latin American Republics
polities.desc: The independent states of the Americas in 1900: Mexico under Porfirio Díaz's dictatorship; Argentina in the middle of its European-immigration boom; Brazil eleven years into its republic; Chile recovering from the War of the Pacific; Colombia about to lose Panama. Economies pegged to one or two export commodities — Argentine beef, Chilean nitrates, Brazilian coffee, Colombian bananas — and dominated by British and American capital.

name: The Great War
desc: Four years of industrial slaughter end with four empires gone — Hohenzollern, Habsburg, Romanov, Ottoman. Ten million dead in uniform, perhaps seven million civilians, plus fifty to a hundred million in the influenza pandemic of 1918–19. The map of Europe and the Middle East redrawn at Versailles will last, with adjustments, into our present.

events.name: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
events.desc: June 28, 1914. Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, shoots the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne on the Latin Bridge in Sarajevo. Within five weeks the alliance systems pull Austria-Hungary, Russia, Germany, France, Britain, and the Ottoman Empire into general war. The 19th century ends here.

events.name: Battle of the Somme
events.desc: July 1 – November 18, 1916. Over a million casualties across the five-month offensive on a twenty-mile front in Picardy. 57,000 British casualties on the first day alone — still the worst day in British military history. The tank makes its combat debut. Kitchener's volunteer armies are ground up; conscription follows.

events.name: Sykes-Picot Agreement
events.desc: Britain and France secretly partition the Ottoman Arab provinces between them. France gets Syria and Lebanon; Britain gets Palestine, Transjordan, and Iraq. Contradicts simultaneous British promises to the Sharif of Mecca and the Balfour Declaration's pledge to Jewish Zionists. The three incompatible commitments become the structural problem of the modern Middle East.

events.name: Balfour Declaration
events.desc: November 2, 1917. Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour writes Lord Rothschild that His Majesty's Government 'view with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people.' The first great-power endorsement of Zionism. Seventy-six words that set the twentieth century's Middle East on its trajectory.

events.name: American entry into the war
events.desc: April 6, 1917. Wilson asks Congress to declare war on Germany after the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram. Two million doughboys in France by 1918 tip the balance. The United States emerges as the decisive industrial and financial power; Wilson's Fourteen Points define the postwar settlement's ideology, though not its practice.

events.name: Treaty of Versailles
events.desc: June 28, 1919, the Hall of Mirrors, five years to the day after Sarajevo. The treaty strips Germany of 13 percent of its territory and 10 percent of its population, demands reparations of £6.6 billion, and assigns sole war guilt via Article 231. Keynes, walking out in disgust, predicts within months that the terms will produce another war. The League of Nations is founded in the same document; the US Senate refuses to join.

events.name: Armenian Genocide
events.desc: The Young Turk government of the Ottoman Empire deports and massacres perhaps 1.2 million Armenians in the eastern Anatolian provinces between April 1915 and 1918. The first modern genocide of the century — a template the Holocaust will later echo. Turkey has not officially acknowledged it to this day.

events.name: 1918 influenza pandemic
events.desc: H1N1 influenza, probably originating in military camps in Kansas or the Western Front, kills 50 to 100 million people in four waves through 1920 — more than the war itself. Young adults die disproportionately. Wartime censorship suppresses reporting outside neutral Spain (hence the name 'Spanish flu'). The first modern pandemic of a connected world.

events.name: Russian Revolution
events.desc: February 1917 — the tsar abdicates. October 1917 — Bolsheviks storm the Winter Palace. Lenin sues for peace at Brest-Litovsk in 1918, losing Finland, the Baltics, Poland, Ukraine, and the Caucasus to secure Bolshevik rule. Civil war rages until 1922. The first Marxist state is created out of tsarist collapse — the twentieth century's second founding act, after the war itself.

polities.name: Central Powers
polities.desc: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria. Held two fronts for four years. By November 1918 all four governments collapse: kaiser, emperor, sultan, and tsar are gone within fifteen months. The Hohenzollern, Habsburg, Romanov, and Ottoman imperial orders — some a thousand years old — end in a single cataclysm.
polities.note: The four-empire collapse of 1917–22 is the largest political erasure in modern history.

polities.name: Entente & Allied Powers
polities.desc: Britain, France, Russia (until 1917), Italy (from 1915), Japan, and the United States (from 1917). Emerge victorious but exhausted. Britain and France retain their empires through the mandate system; Italy is disappointed at Versailles; Japan collects German Pacific possessions; America turns isolationist. Russia's exit in 1917 becomes the largest political transformation of all.

polities.name: United States (belated belligerent)
polities.desc: Wilson leads the country into war in April 1917 after three years of formal neutrality. Two million American soldiers in France by November 1918. The AEF under Pershing is the decisive reserve that exhausts the last German spring offensive. At Versailles, Wilson's Fourteen Points are gutted by the European victors; the Senate rejects the League of Nations; America retreats into interwar isolationism.

polities.name: Russian Revolution / Civil War
polities.desc: The tsar abdicates in March 1917; the Bolsheviks seize power in November. Lenin signs the humiliating Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 — Finland, the Baltics, Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, and the Caucasus lost to secure Bolshevik survival. Civil war then tears the country apart for five years. The Reds win; the USSR is founded in 1922. The first Marxist-Leninist state inherits a population in famine and a state apparatus built from revolutionary improvisation.

polities.name: Spain (neutral)
polities.desc: Alfonso XIII's Spain maintains neutrality and profits from supplying both sides. The post-1898 national fatigue has not lifted; Catalan and Basque regional movements are organizing; the working-class left is radicalizing under anarchist and socialist banners. Primo de Rivera's dictatorship is six years away; the Civil War eighteen.

polities.name: Other Neutrals
polities.desc: The Netherlands, the Scandinavian kingdoms, Switzerland, Persia (nominally, though Russian and British troops fought across it), Ethiopia, Siam (which joined the Entente in 1917), and most of Latin America stay out or contribute only symbolically. Neutrality in a total war between empires is itself a form of alignment.

name: Fascism Rising
desc: Hitler has been Chancellor for three years, Mussolini for fourteen. Spain descends into civil war in July. Japan has seized Manchuria and is building toward full war with China. Stalin's purges begin in earnest. The League of Nations has failed; the democracies are paralyzed. The Second World War is, in retrospect, already underway.

events.name: Mussolini's March on Rome
events.desc: October 28, 1922. Forty thousand Blackshirts converge on Rome; King Victor Emmanuel III, rather than order the army to disperse them, invites Mussolini to form a government. Il Duce is thirty-nine. Within four years the Fascist state is consolidated — opposition parties banned, press controlled, parliament neutered. The template for every subsequent interwar fascism, including Hitler's, is set in Italy first.

events.name: Hitler becomes Chancellor
events.desc: January 30, 1933. Paul von Hindenburg appoints Hitler Chancellor of Germany. Within six months the Reichstag Fire Decree suspends civil liberties, the Enabling Act makes Hitler dictator, the SPD and KPD are outlawed, and the first concentration camp opens at Dachau. By August 1934 Hindenburg is dead and Hitler is Führer. A modern industrial democracy disassembles itself in twenty months.

events.name: Japanese invasion of Manchuria
events.desc: September 18, 1931. The Mukden Incident — Japanese Kwantung Army officers stage a bombing on the South Manchuria Railway and use it as pretext to seize the entire region. The puppet state of Manchukuo is proclaimed in 1932 with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as figurehead. The League of Nations condemns the aggression; Japan walks out. The first revisionist power to defy the Versailles system does so without consequence — and is watched closely from Rome and Berlin.

events.name: Italy invades Ethiopia
events.desc: October 1935. Mussolini's armies invade Ethiopia from Eritrea and Italian Somaliland, using mustard gas and aerial bombardment to overcome the last independent African state. Haile Selassie's appeal to the League of Nations is heard but not answered. Sanctions are half-hearted; the British and French appease Mussolini to keep him out of Hitler's orbit. The League's credibility is broken; four years later Mussolini and Hitler sign the Pact of Steel.

events.name: Spanish Civil War
events.desc: July 18, 1936. Nationalist generals led by Francisco Franco revolt against the Popular Front Republic. Three years of war: Italian and German troops and aircraft on the Nationalist side, Soviet arms and the International Brigades for the Republic. Guernica is bombed by the Condor Legion on April 26, 1937. The democracies maintain a non-intervention fiction that benefits only Franco. By April 1939 the Republic has fallen; 500,000 dead; Franco rules for thirty-six years. The dress rehearsal for the greater war.

events.name: Anschluss
events.desc: March 12, 1938. Wehrmacht troops cross into Austria; Hitler returns to his birthplace in triumph; a plebiscite ratifies union at 99.7 percent. The first territorial revision of the Versailles order absorbed without a shot. Six months later the Sudeten crisis; by March 1939 all of Czechoslovakia is gone. Chamberlain returns from Munich with 'peace for our time.'

events.name: Second Sino-Japanese War
events.desc: The Marco Polo Bridge Incident of July 7, 1937 escalates into full war. By December, Nanjing has fallen; six weeks of mass murder and rape follow — perhaps 300,000 Chinese civilians killed. Chiang retreats to Chongqing; the Communists regroup in Yan'an. The Pacific theater of the Second World War has effectively begun, four years before Pearl Harbor. By 1945 perhaps 20 million Chinese will be dead.

events.name: Stalin's Great Purge
events.desc: 1936–38. Show trials of old Bolsheviks (Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin); mass arrests by the NKVD; perhaps 700,000 executed outright and hundreds of thousands more dying in the Gulag. The Red Army officer corps is decimated — three of five marshals, fifteen of sixteen army commanders, half the colonels — just as war approaches. Stalin pays for it in blood two years later against the Wehrmacht.

polities.name: Nazi Germany
polities.desc: Hitler's Third Reich. The Rhineland remilitarized (1936), Austria annexed (1938), Czechoslovakia dismembered (1938–39). Wehrmacht rearmament at scale. Nuremberg Laws codify racial categories. Jewish emigration rises; concentration camps are still for political prisoners but will soon be for more. Four-Year Plan gears the economy for war.

polities.name: Fascist Italy
polities.desc: Mussolini's regime in its fourteenth year. The Italian Empire has just absorbed Ethiopia (1936). Libya is being 'pacified' with concentration camps (100,000 dead); Albania will be annexed in 1939. The Axis with Germany is signed in October 1936; Hitler calls it 'the Rome-Berlin Axis.' The Roman imperial aesthetic — fasces, eagles, monumental architecture — is now the official register of the Italian state.

polities.name: Imperial Japan
polities.desc: The Kwantung Army has effectively annexed Manchuria as Manchukuo. The assassination of moderates in the February 26 Incident (1936) finishes the civilian government's authority over the military. Full-scale war with China begins July 1937. The Imperial Japanese Navy is building the world's largest battleships (Yamato, Musashi); the Imperial Japanese Army looks to Siberia and Southeast Asia.

polities.name: Nationalist Spain
polities.desc: Franco's insurgent Nationalists — army, Church, monarchists, Carlists, Falangists — have taken Seville, Cádiz, and the western half of the country by late 1936 with German and Italian air support. The Condor Legion flies for Franco; Italian CTV divisions fight alongside him. Madrid holds out until March 1939. The Nationalist victory will install a clerical-fascist regime for the next thirty-six years.

polities.name: Spanish Republic
polities.desc: The Popular Front government — socialists, communists, anarchists, Catalan nationalists, liberal republicans — defends itself with Soviet arms, International Brigade volunteers (35,000 from 50 countries including 2,800 Americans of the Lincoln Battalion), and the industrial workers of Madrid and Barcelona. Internal fratricide between communists and anarchists (POUM, CNT) weakens the effort. The last democracy in continental Europe south of Scandinavia is strangled over thirty-three months.

polities.name: Soviet Union (under Stalin)
polities.desc: Collectivization (1928–33) has killed perhaps five million, mostly Ukrainians in the Holodomor. The Five-Year Plans are industrializing at breakneck cost. The Great Purge (1936–38) decapitates the party, army, and intelligentsia. The Popular Front line with Western communists against fascism runs simultaneously. In 1939 Stalin will stun the world by signing a pact with Hitler.

polities.name: Western Democracies
polities.desc: Britain under Baldwin (then Chamberlain from 1937), France under the Popular Front of Léon Blum, the United States under Roosevelt's New Deal. All three are turned inward — recovering from the Depression, politically cautious, militarily unprepared. Appeasement is the logical response to publics that above all do not want another 1914–18. That caution will cost Czechoslovakia in 1938 and Poland in 1939.

polities.name: Republic of China (KMT)
polities.desc: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government has nominally reunified China since 1928, but warlords still run large chunks of the interior and the Japanese hold the northeast. Full-scale war with Japan begins in July 1937 with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident; Nanjing falls in December; the capital is moved first to Wuhan, then to Chongqing.

polities.name: Latin American Republics
polities.desc: Mexico under Cárdenas (Popular Front-adjacent) nationalizes oil in 1938; Brazil under Vargas's Estado Novo (1937) becomes a corporatist semi-fascist state; Argentina oscillates between oligarchy and military coups. The hemisphere is split between the sympathies of military elites (often pro-Axis) and working-class mass movements (often anti-fascist).

name: Axis High Tide
desc: The peak territorial extent of the Axis powers. German armies are at Stalingrad and El Alamein. Japan controls a Pacific empire from Burma to the Solomons.

events.name: Battle of Stalingrad
events.desc: The five-month battle (August 1942 – February 1943) that breaks the Wehrmacht. German Sixth Army of 300,000 is destroyed or captured. The strategic turning point of the European war — Germany will never again mount a major offensive in the East.

events.name: Battle of Midway
events.desc: Four Japanese fleet carriers sunk in a single day by US naval aviation. The strategic turning point of the Pacific war, six months after Pearl Harbor. Japan loses its trained carrier pilots and its offensive capability simultaneously.

events.name: Second Battle of El Alamein
events.desc: Montgomery's Eighth Army breaks Rommel's Afrika Korps. Churchill: 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.' North Africa is secured; the invasion of Italy becomes possible.

events.name: Wannsee Conference
events.desc: Senior Nazi officials meet at a villa outside Berlin to coordinate the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question.' The bureaucratic formalization of genocide already underway. Over the next three years six million Jews and millions of others will be murdered.

polities.name: Greater German Reich
polities.desc: Direct rule or occupation from the Atlantic to the Volga, and across North Africa to the gates of El Alamein with Rommel's Afrika Korps. The Wehrmacht's high-water mark. Within months Stalingrad will reverse the tide.
polities.note: The most concentrated attempt in modern history to overturn the Westphalian system by force.

polities.name: Soviet Union
polities.desc: Reduced by invasion to roughly two-thirds of its territory but mobilizing on a scale the Reich cannot match. Industrial capacity is being relocated to the Urals; Leningrad is besieged; Moscow's government partly evacuated to Kuibyshev. The Central Asian and Caucasian republics are feeding the war economy; Siberian divisions transferred from the Manchurian frontier will turn the battle for Moscow.

polities.name: Empire of Japan
polities.desc: The Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere extends from Manchuria to the Solomons. A Pacific empire built on naval aviation. Manchukuo (since 1931), Korea (since 1910), Taiwan (since 1895); the Dutch East Indies, French Indochina, British Malaya, the Philippines, and most of China's coast and Yangtze basin under direct or puppet rule.

polities.name: Kingdom of Italy (Fascist)
polities.desc: Mussolini's Italy, allied with Germany since the Pact of Steel (1939). Libya is the 'Fourth Shore'; Albania was annexed in 1939. The Italian East African empire — Ethiopia, Eritrea, Italian Somaliland — was lost to the British in 1941. The Regio Esercito is fighting alongside the Wehrmacht in North Africa and Russia; the Regia Marina is bottled up in the Mediterranean. By September 1943 Italy will surrender and split between a German-occupied north and an Allied-liberated south.

polities.name: Francoist Spain (neutral)
polities.desc: Franco's Nationalists won the Civil War in 1939 with decisive German and Italian help. Spain is formally non-belligerent but sympathetic to the Axis — Franco met Hitler at Hendaye in October 1940 but declined to enter the war; the Blue Division of Spanish volunteers fights for Germany on the Eastern Front. Spanish Morocco, the Sahara, and Equatorial Guinea remain colonies. The regime will survive until Franco's death in 1975.

polities.name: Vichy France
polities.desc: Pétain's État Français has governed the unoccupied southern zone of France and the French empire since the armistice of June 1940. In November 1942, responding to the Allied landings in North Africa (Operation Torch), Germany occupies the southern zone; Vichy becomes a shell. French West Africa defects to the Free French; Indochina remains in Vichy/Japanese co-administration.

polities.name: Communist China (Yan'an)
polities.desc: Mao Zedong's Communist Party, driven from Jiangxi in 1934 by Chiang's encirclement campaigns, arrived in Shaanxi after the Long March in 1935. Yan'an is now the headquarters of a guerrilla state of some 90 million people behind Japanese lines. The Second United Front with the KMT is nominal; the real struggle is for the postwar peasant constituency. Within seven years Mao will enter Beijing.

polities.name: British Empire (war footing)
polities.desc: Diminished but still vast. India, Australia, Canada, and Africa are mobilizing for total war. The Middle East mandates — Palestine, Transjordan, Iraq — anchor the Suez-to-Basra oil corridor; Iran has been jointly occupied with the Soviets since August 1941 to secure the Persian Corridor for Lend-Lease to Russia. The empire's last great military effort.

polities.name: United States
polities.desc: Mobilizing the largest war economy in history. By war's end will produce more than half of global manufacturing output.

polities.name: Free China (KMT)
polities.desc: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government has retreated to Sichuan behind the Yangtze gorges. Ruling from Chongqing under sustained Japanese bombing, Chiang ties down perhaps a million Japanese troops while receiving Allied supplies over the Hump from Assam. The Burma Road is cut; American Lend-Lease flows in through the air. The KMT holds the southwestern interior — Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, most of Hunan and Guangxi, western Hubei, Xinjiang, and Tibet nominally.

name: War's End — Occupation
desc: VE Day in May; VJ Day in September. Germany, Austria, and Korea are divided into occupation zones; Japan is under American supervision. The shape of the Cold War is being drawn on the ground by the armies that arrive first. This map shows occupation zones rather than sovereign states.

events.name: Hiroshima
events.desc: August 6, 1945. The uranium bomb 'Little Boy' detonates 1,900 feet above Hiroshima. Roughly 70,000 killed instantly; the total death toll by year's end reaches 140,000. Three days later Nagasaki. Six days after Nagasaki, Japan surrenders. The atomic age begins.

events.name: Yalta Conference
events.desc: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin meet in Crimea to plan the postwar order. Agreements on occupation zones in Germany, the UN, and Soviet entry into the Pacific war. The territorial compromises effectively concede Eastern Europe to Soviet control.

events.name: D-Day
events.desc: Operation Overlord: 156,000 Allied troops land on the Normandy beaches on June 6, 1944. The largest amphibious invasion in history opens the Western Front. Within eleven months the Wehrmacht surrenders unconditionally.

events.name: Fall of Berlin
events.desc: The Red Army takes Berlin after a three-week battle costing 81,000 Soviet and perhaps 100,000 German lives. Hitler commits suicide on April 30. Germany surrenders on May 8. The Soviet position in central Europe is established by the fact of military presence.

events.name: Founding of the United Nations
events.desc: The UN Charter is signed in San Francisco by 50 nations on June 26, 1945. The Security Council's five permanent members with veto power — US, USSR, UK, France, China — formalize the postwar great-power hierarchy that will structure international politics for the next eight decades.

events.name: Aramco concession
events.desc: Standard Oil of California secures exclusive rights to prospect for oil across Saudi Arabia from Ibn Saud for £50,000 in gold. In 1938 Dammam Well No. 7 strikes commercial quantities. Aramco will become the most valuable industrial enterprise in history.

events.name: Seven Sisters era
events.desc: Mossadegh nationalizes Anglo-Iranian Oil; the British and Americans overthrow him in 1953. The 'Seven Sisters' — Exxon, Mobil, Chevron, Texaco, Gulf, BP, Shell — control about 85 percent of world oil reserves until OPEC breaks their grip in the 1970s.

events.name: Ghawar field discovered
events.desc: Aramco geologists confirm the Ghawar field in the Saudi Eastern Province — the largest conventional oil field ever discovered. 280 kilometers long, 30 wide, 70 billion barrels recovered to date with perhaps another 40 to go. Ghawar alone has produced more oil than any country except Saudi Arabia itself. For seventy years its output quietly sets the floor of world oil supply; when it finally begins to decline in the 2020s, Aramco's IPO prospectus is the first document to admit it. The single most consequential geological feature of the 20th century.

events.name: Hoover Dam completed
events.desc: 221 meters of concrete across Black Canyon on the Colorado River, dedicated by Roosevelt in 1935 — the largest concrete structure on earth at the time. The dam electrifies Los Angeles, creates Lake Mead, makes the desert Southwest habitable at scale, and inaugurates the era of big-state infrastructure: the TVA, the Grand Coulee, Glen Canyon, the Aswan High Dam, China's Three Gorges. 96 workers died in the construction. Every later dispute over Western water — and there are many more coming — traces back to the allocation compact signed around its pouring.

events.name: First transistor
events.desc: At Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey, on December 23, 1947, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley demonstrate a working point-contact transistor — a solid-state amplifier that replaces the vacuum tube. Within a decade the transistor is shrunk onto silicon; within two, Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce build the integrated circuit. Everything digital, from the mainframe to the smartphone to the GPU training frontier models, is a direct descendant of this device. The most consequential invention of the 20th century.

events.name: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'
events.desc: Alan Turing publishes 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' in Mind, opening with the question 'Can machines think?' He replaces it with the imitation game — what becomes the Turing test — and predicts that by 2000 machines will play it well enough to fool most interrogators thirty percent of the time. Off by a few decades but correct in principle. The founding document of artificial intelligence as a research program. Turing is prosecuted for homosexuality in 1952 and dies in 1954 at 41.

events.name: Interstate Highway System
events.desc: Eisenhower signs the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, authorizing 66,000 kilometers of controlled-access highway at a cost of $25 billion — the largest public-works project in American history. Justified in Cold War terms as an evacuation and mobilization system, it remakes the country: the suburbs, the trucking industry, the collapse of passenger rail, the hollowing of downtowns, the logistics geography that Walmart and Amazon later inherit. Eisenhower said he got the idea from the German Autobahn in 1919 and again in 1945.

polities.name: Soviet Occupation Zone
polities.desc: The Red Army occupies East Germany, Austria's eastern half, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, the Baltics, and northern Korea. Most will become Communist satellites within three years. The iron curtain is being drawn.
polities.note: The geographical distribution of Allied armies in May 1945 determined the political geography of Europe for the next forty-five years. Where the Red Army stopped, the Warsaw Pact began.

polities.name: US Occupation Zone
polities.desc: US forces occupy southern Germany, western Austria, southern Korea, Japan, Okinawa, and the Philippines. MacArthur governs Japan as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. The Marshall Plan and Bretton Woods institutions are being designed.
polities.note: The continental United States is the only major industrial power to emerge from the war with its infrastructure untouched and its economy doubled in size.

polities.name: British Occupation Zone
polities.desc: Britain occupies northwestern Germany, northern Italy, Greece, and parts of the former Italian empire. Attlee's Labour government is elected in July. The empire is bankrupt; India will be independent within two years.

polities.name: French Occupation Zone
polities.desc: De Gaulle's provisional government occupies southwestern Germany, and reclaims Indochina and North Africa. The Fourth Republic is being founded. The empire will not survive the next decade — Indochina leaves in 1954, Algeria in 1962.

polities.name: Nationalist China (victorious)
polities.desc: Chiang Kai-shek has nominal control of China and is recognized as one of the Big Four. The reality is that the civil war with Mao's Communists is about to reopen; the Nationalists will lose the mainland within four years.

polities.name: Yugoslavia (Tito)
polities.desc: Tito's Partisans liberated the country themselves, not the Red Army. This will let Yugoslavia break with Stalin in 1948 and pursue nonaligned socialism — the only Communist state in Europe outside Moscow's bloc.

polities.name: Neutral Nations
polities.desc: Sweden, Switzerland, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Turkey stayed out of the war. Most emerge with their institutions intact while the belligerent powers rebuild. Sweden will host European industrial renewal; Switzerland will be the financial center of the reconstruction.

polities.name: New Caledonia (French)

name: Height of the Cold War
desc: The bipolar system at its peak. Two nuclear superpowers, two blocs, two economic systems, two visions of modernity. Between the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, the Cold War is fought everywhere at once — proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola, Nicaragua; a space race from Sputnik to the Moon; an ideological war on campuses from Berkeley to Prague; a nuclear arms race that peaks at 70,000 warheads. China breaks with Moscow and then with itself in the Cultural Revolution; Nixon flies to Beijing; OPEC seizes the oil. The Third World is a prize to be contested.

events.name: Korean War
events.desc: June 25, 1950. Kim Il-sung's Korean People's Army crosses the 38th parallel with Stalin's approval. Seoul falls in three days. The UN (with the USSR boycotting the Security Council) authorizes intervention; MacArthur's Inchon landing reverses the tide; the Chinese Volunteer Army crosses the Yalu in November and drives the UN back to the parallel. Three years of trench warfare along roughly the 38th. Armistice signed at Panmunjom in July 1953; no peace treaty to this day. Three million Koreans dead, a country permanently divided, 28,000 American troops still in the South seventy-three years later. The first hot war of the Cold War and the template for every proxy conflict that follows.

events.name: Suez Crisis
events.desc: Nasser nationalizes the Suez Canal in July. Britain, France, and Israel launch a secret joint invasion in October. Eisenhower, furious at the Anglo-French move without US consultation and at the disastrous timing during the Hungarian crisis, forces a humiliating withdrawal by threatening the pound sterling. Britain's imperial pretensions effectively end here; Nasser becomes the hero of pan-Arab nationalism; the US replaces the old colonial powers as the dominant extra-regional force in the Middle East.

events.name: Hungarian Revolution
events.desc: October–November 1956. A student-led uprising in Budapest overthrows the Stalinist government. Imre Nagy declares neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. Khrushchev, after initial hesitation, orders 200,000 Soviet troops and 2,500 tanks into Hungary. Perhaps 20,000 Hungarians dead, 200,000 refugees fleeing west. Nagy executed in 1958. The Western powers, distracted by Suez and unwilling to risk nuclear war, do nothing. The limits of 'rollback' are established; the Brezhnev Doctrine takes shape.

events.name: Sputnik and the Space Race
events.desc: October 4, 1957. An R-7 rocket from Baikonur puts an 84-kilogram aluminum sphere into orbit, beeping on shortwave every 96 minutes. The American shock is total. Eisenhower creates NASA and ARPA within months. Yuri Gagarin orbits the earth in April 1961. Kennedy commits to the Moon six weeks later. The space race — simultaneously a scientific, ideological, and military competition, since every rocket that launches a satellite can launch a warhead — defines the next fifteen years of technology policy. Apollo 11 lands in July 1969; the Soviet N-1 rocket fails four times; the USSR never quite catches up after that single October morning.

events.name: Bay of Pigs
events.desc: April 17, 1961. A CIA-trained brigade of 1,400 Cuban exiles lands at the Bay of Pigs on the southern coast of Cuba, intending to trigger a general uprising against Castro. Kennedy withholds promised air cover. The invaders are crushed in three days. The humiliation radicalizes Castro — he declares himself a Marxist-Leninist in December — and sets up the confrontation that becomes the Missile Crisis eighteen months later.

events.name: Berlin Wall erected
events.desc: Overnight on August 13, 1961, East German troops begin stringing barbed wire along the sector boundary in Berlin. Within weeks a concrete wall replaces it. 3.5 million East Germans had fled west through Berlin since 1945 — a hemorrhage the GDR could not survive. The wall stops the flow; it also becomes the iconic image of the Cold War for the next 28 years. Kennedy at the Brandenburg Gate in 1963: 'Ich bin ein Berliner.' Reagan at the same spot in 1987: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.' It comes down on November 9, 1989.

events.name: Cuban Missile Crisis
events.desc: October 14–28, 1962. U-2 reconnaissance photos show Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles being installed in Cuba. Kennedy orders a naval 'quarantine' rather than the airstrike favored by the Joint Chiefs. For thirteen days the world comes closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in its history — on October 27, a US destroyer drops warning charges on a Soviet B-59 submarine unaware that the sub is armed with a nuclear torpedo and that only the intervention of executive officer Vasily Arkhipov prevents its launch. Khrushchev withdraws the missiles in exchange for a public US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret pledge to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Both leaders, sobered, establish the Moscow-Washington hotline in 1963 and sign the Partial Test Ban Treaty the same year.

events.name: Sino-Soviet Split
events.desc: The ideological break between Moscow and Beijing, visible by 1956 and public by 1960. Mao denounces Khrushchev's 'revisionism' and peaceful coexistence with the West; Khrushchev withdraws all Soviet technicians and aid from China in August 1960. By 1969 Soviet and Chinese troops are shooting at each other along the Ussuri River at Zhenbao Island. The split shatters the Communist monolith and opens the diplomatic space that Nixon and Kissinger will exploit in 1971–72. Mao's willingness to court the United States against the USSR reshapes the geometry of the Cold War more than any event since 1945.

events.name: Cultural Revolution
events.desc: May 1966. Mao launches the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution to reassert control after the catastrophe of the Great Leap Forward (30+ million dead, 1959–61). Red Guards attack teachers, intellectuals, 'capitalist roaders,' and ultimately the Party itself. Liu Shaoqi dies in prison; Deng Xiaoping is purged; universities close for a decade; perhaps 1.5 to 2 million die, tens of millions persecuted. The destruction of Chinese cultural and institutional capital is vast. Mao dies in 1976; the Gang of Four is arrested within weeks; Deng returns in 1978 with the reform-and-opening program that will make China the world's industrial base.

events.name: Tet Offensive
events.desc: January 30, 1968. During the Vietnamese Lunar New Year truce, the North Vietnamese Army and Viet Cong launch simultaneous attacks on more than 100 South Vietnamese cities. They are militarily defeated — most gains recaptured within weeks — but the images of fighting in Saigon and at the US embassy destroy American public confidence that the war is being won. Walter Cronkite: 'we are mired in stalemate.' Johnson declines to seek re-election in March. The war grinds on for seven more years. Saigon falls in April 1975. Three million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans dead.

events.name: Prague Spring
events.desc: January–August 1968. Alexander Dubček's reformist Czechoslovak government attempts 'socialism with a human face' — press freedom, economic decentralization, political pluralism inside Communist forms. On the night of August 20–21, 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops invade. No meaningful resistance; Dubček is arrested and taken to Moscow. The Brezhnev Doctrine — Moscow's right to intervene in any socialist country straying from the line — is publicly articulated in its wake. The reformist Communist project in Eastern Europe is effectively dead until 1989.

events.name: Apollo 11 — Moon landing
events.desc: July 20, 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land the Lunar Module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility; Michael Collins orbits above. 600 million people watch live — a fifth of humanity. The program costs $25 billion (perhaps $260 billion in 2025 terms) and employs 400,000 people. Kennedy's 1961 challenge — 'before this decade is out' — is met with five months to spare. The geopolitical meaning is unmistakable: the United States has decisively won the space race, eleven years and nine months after Sputnik. Five more Apollo missions land between 1969 and 1972; then nothing. No human returns to the Moon for 53 years.

events.name: Nixon in China
events.desc: February 21–28, 1972. Richard Nixon, the arch-anti-Communist of 1950s American politics, shakes hands with Mao Zedong in Beijing. Henry Kissinger has secretly negotiated the opening through Pakistan the previous year. The Shanghai Communiqué acknowledges 'one China' while fudging Taiwan's status. The diplomatic revolution isolates Moscow, pressures Hanoi toward the Paris accords, and begins the three-decade process that will make China the workshop of the world and the United States' primary creditor. Until 1971 the PRC was not even a member of the UN; by 2010 it is the world's second-largest economy.

events.name: Yom Kippur War and OPEC embargo
events.desc: October 6, 1973. Egypt and Syria attack Israel on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar. Initial Arab gains across the Suez Canal and on the Golan Heights are reversed within two weeks; a US emergency airlift (Operation Nickel Grass) resupplies the IDF. Brezhnev threatens intervention; Nixon raises DEFCON 3; the crisis passes. The Arab OPEC members embargo the US and Netherlands in retaliation; oil prices quadruple in three months. The postwar Western boom ends. Stagflation, deindustrialization, and the politics of scarcity begin. The petrodollar system is born. The Middle East's centrality to the world economy is established for the next fifty years.

events.name: Fall of Saigon
events.desc: April 30, 1975. North Vietnamese T-54 tanks crash through the gates of the Presidential Palace in Saigon. Operation Frequent Wind — the helicopter evacuation from the US embassy rooftop — ends American involvement in mainland Southeast Asia after thirty years and 58,000 dead. Within three weeks Cambodia and Laos also fall to Communist forces. The 'domino theory' appears vindicated; it will look less so within a decade as Vietnam and China fight a border war in 1979, and as Deng's China opens to the West. The last great Communist expansion; also the high-water mark of Soviet influence in Asia.

events.name: Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
events.desc: December 24–27, 1979. Soviet airborne forces seize Kabul airport; the KGB assassinates President Hafizullah Amin inside the Presidential Palace; Babrak Karmal is installed. Moscow expects a brief stabilization operation; it becomes a nine-year counterinsurgency against the CIA-armed, Saudi-funded, Pakistan-based mujahideen. 15,000 Soviet dead, perhaps a million Afghan. Stinger missiles from 1986 neutralize Soviet airpower. Gorbachev withdraws in February 1989. The war is the Soviet Vietnam — the demonstration that the empire has overreached — and arguably accelerates the collapse that follows two years later. It also incubates the jihadist networks that will hit the World Trade Center twelve years after the Soviets leave.

events.name: Singapore independence
events.desc: August 9, 1965. Singapore is expelled from the Federation of Malaysia after two years of political conflict. Lee Kuan Yew announces independence on television, tears in his eyes — he had believed the merger was his city's only viable future. Over the next three decades the PAP-governed city-state pursues export-led industrialization, public housing, rigorous English-language education, and ruthless meritocracy; per-capita GDP rises from that of a poor country to among the highest in the world. Singapore becomes the model invoked from Dubai to Rwanda to Shenzhen — the developmental authoritarian case study of the post-colonial era.

polities.name: Soviet Union & Warsaw Pact
polities.desc: Brezhnev presides over the peak of Soviet power: the strategic parity of SALT I, the client states from Havana to Hanoi, the second-largest economy on earth. The Brezhnev Doctrine (1968) asserts Moscow's right to intervene anywhere socialism is threatened. Beneath the surface: stagnating productivity, a creaking central plan, the slow realization that the West is pulling away in computers, consumer goods, and agricultural yields. The rot that will collapse the system by 1991 is already setting in.
polities.note: At its 1970s peak the USSR projected power to every continent. A generation later, only Russia would remain, and it would be smaller than it had been in 1914.

polities.name: United States & NATO
polities.desc: Containment in its mature form. NATO under SACEUR runs from Norway to eastern Turkey, fielding roughly 4 million troops against a Warsaw Pact of similar scale. The American nuclear umbrella covers Western Europe, Japan, South Korea, and Australia. Domestic turmoil — civil rights, Vietnam, Watergate, stagflation — does not, on the whole, translate into strategic retreat. The alliance that was built against Stalin outlives every Soviet premier and will still be operating against Russia in 2022.
polities.note: History's first genuinely multilateral military alliance among equals — held together less by fear of invasion than by shared commitment to a liberal economic and political order.

polities.name: People's Republic of China
polities.desc: The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) has shattered Party institutions and killed perhaps 1.5 million people. Mao receives Nixon in 1972 — an event unthinkable five years earlier — tilting China away from Moscow in a diplomatic revolution that reshapes the global balance. After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping sidelines the Gang of Four and in 1978 launches Reform and Opening. Agricultural decollectivization, the Special Economic Zones at Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Xiamen, and Shantou, and the opening to Japanese and Western investment set up the four decades of growth that make China the world's manufacturing core.

polities.name: Non-Aligned Movement
polities.desc: Founded at the 1955 Bandung Conference and institutionalized at Belgrade in 1961 by Tito, Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno, and Nkrumah. By the 1970s over 100 member states, mostly postcolonial. In principle a refusal to choose between the superpowers; in practice a spectrum running from the genuinely neutral (Yugoslavia, India, Sweden in spirit) to Soviet-aligned (Cuba, Angola) to Western-aligned (Saudi Arabia until the 1990s). The movement's real importance is demographic: the majority of humanity lives under governments that declined to be either side's satellite.

polities.name: Communist Indochina
polities.desc: North Vietnam under Le Duan (Ho having died in 1969) finally unifies the country after the Fall of Saigon in April 1975. Laos falls to the Pathet Lao in December 1975. Cambodia falls to Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge in April 1975 — the Year Zero regime will kill 1.5 to 2 million in less than four years before Vietnam invades and deposes it in January 1979. China, angered, attacks Vietnam in February 1979; the two-week border war is a PLA debacle that convinces Deng that the army urgently needs modernization.

polities.name: Cuba
polities.desc: Castro's Cuba, Soviet-aligned since 1961, survives the Bay of Pigs, the Missile Crisis, and the US embargo through massive Soviet subsidies. In the 1970s Havana becomes an improbable military expeditionary power — 30,000 Cuban troops fight for the MPLA in Angola from 1975; others deploy to Ethiopia in 1977 against Somalia. Soviet subsidies keep the economy afloat; when they stop in 1991 the 'Special Period' of malnutrition and blackouts begins.

polities.name: Imperial Iran (Shah)
polities.desc: Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi rules a modernizing, oil-rich, Washington-aligned Iran. The 'White Revolution' (1963) — land reform, female suffrage, literacy corps — has the full backing of the Kennedy administration. By the mid-1970s Iran is the largest military power in the Persian Gulf; the Shah imagines it as the fifth industrial power of the world within a generation. SAVAK's torture chambers, the conspicuous consumption of the court, and the alienation of both the bazaar and the clergy set up the revolution of 1979 that ends the dynasty and the alliance in a single stroke.

polities.name: Gulf Monarchies (pre-petrodollar)
polities.desc: Faisal of Saudi Arabia has quadrupled oil prices in 1973 and become, almost overnight, one of the most important men in the world. The Gulf monarchies remain pro-Western in alignment but use oil as a political weapon. The petrodollar recycling system — OPEC prices in dollars, surpluses deposited in Western banks — ties the House of Saud to the Federal Reserve in a partnership that lasts to the present.

polities.name: Apartheid South Africa & Rhodesia
polities.desc: Pretoria under Vorster and then Botha; Ian Smith's Rhodesia since the 1965 Unilateral Declaration of Independence. Both backed quietly by the West as Cold War frontline states against Soviet-supported liberation movements (ANC/MK, ZANU, ZAPU, SWAPO, FRELIMO, MPLA). South African forces intervene in Angola from 1975 against Cuban troops; the stalemate lasts until the 1988 Tripartite Agreement. Rhodesia becomes Zimbabwe in 1980; South African apartheid ends in 1994.

polities.name: Portugal (late Estado Novo)
polities.desc: Europe's last colonial empire. Salazar (incapacitated 1968, dies 1970) and Caetano fight three simultaneous colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau from 1961 — draining 40 percent of the national budget and drafting every Portuguese male for four years of Africa service. The Carnation Revolution of April 25, 1974, ends the dictatorship and the empire in one stroke; all five African colonies independent within eighteen months. Portugal joins the EEC in 1986.

polities.name: Spain (late Franco)
polities.desc: Franco's regime in its autumn — he dies in November 1975. Juan Carlos inherits a Spain that transitions peacefully to constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy by 1978. Tacit Western alignment through the 1953 basing agreement; NATO membership comes in 1982, the EEC in 1986. The 'Spanish miracle' of 1960s industrialization and tourism is visible.

polities.name: Indonesia (New Order)
polities.desc: Suharto's New Order, installed by the anti-Communist massacres of 1965–66 (500,000 to 1 million dead) that destroyed the PKI and replaced Sukarno. Closely aligned with Washington during the Cold War; occupies East Timor in 1975 with tacit US approval. Rapid growth, widespread corruption, eventual collapse in the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis.

polities.name: Latin American Dictatorships
polities.desc: Pinochet in Chile (from 1973), the Argentine junta (from 1976), Brazil under the military (1964–85), Paraguay under Stroessner, Uruguay, Bolivia, and the Central American oligarchies. Most backed by Washington as anti-Communist bulwarks under Operation Condor. The Dirty Wars kill tens of thousands and disappear tens of thousands more. Democratization comes, mostly, with the debt crises of the 1980s.

name: End of the Cold War
desc: The Berlin Wall falls. The Soviet bloc dissolves over the next two years. The bipolar world ends; what comes next is contested.

events.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.desc: November 9, 1989. A confused East German press conference announces that travel restrictions are lifted 'immediately.' Crowds gather at the checkpoints; guards stand aside. Within weeks every Eastern European regime except Romania falls without a shot fired.

events.name: Tiananmen Square Massacre
events.desc: June 3–4, 1989. The People's Liberation Army clears Tiananmen Square of pro-democracy protesters. Estimates of deaths range from hundreds to several thousand. The CCP chooses authoritarian economic modernization over political liberalization — the opposite of Gorbachev's gamble.

events.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
events.desc: December 26, 1991. The Supreme Soviet votes itself out of existence. The USSR is formally dissolved into fifteen successor states. The largest state in world history ends peacefully — a historical anomaly.

events.name: Launch of the World Wide Web
events.desc: Tim Berners-Lee publishes the first website at CERN. Within a decade the internet will have restructured global commerce, communications, and politics. The infrastructure of the unipolar moment is as much digital as military.

events.name: OPEC Oil Embargo
events.desc: In retaliation for American support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War, the Arab members of OPEC cut production and embargo the United States and the Netherlands. Oil prices quadruple in three months. Gasoline lines, stagflation, and the end of the postwar boom follow. For the first time the oil-exporting states — not the Seven Sisters majors who set up the industry — control the price of the blood of the industrial economy. The 'petrodollar' system is born: OPEC prices oil in dollars and recycles the surplus through Western banks, tying American monetary power to Saudi export capacity.

events.name: Iranian Revolution
events.desc: The Shah — America's policeman in the Gulf — flees in January. Khomeini returns from exile in February. The hostage crisis at the US embassy (November 1979 – January 1981) destroys Carter's presidency and locks in four decades of US-Iranian enmity. The revolution also removes 5 million barrels per day from world markets overnight, triggering the second oil shock and the recession of the early 1980s. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 is the direct counterpart: Moscow's last southward push, the one that will bleed the empire dry.

events.name: OPEC founded
events.desc: Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, and Venezuela found the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries in Baghdad. The end of the Seven Sisters' pricing monopoly. By 1973 OPEC will hold the industrialized world hostage.

events.name: 1973 Oil Crisis
events.desc: Arab OPEC states embargo the US and the Netherlands for backing Israel in the Yom Kippur War. Oil prices quadruple in months. The end of cheap energy — the Western postwar boom ends; stagflation, deindustrialization, and the politics of scarcity begin. Saudi Arabia becomes the swing producer and central node of the global economy.

events.name: Chernobyl disaster
events.desc: Reactor No. 4 at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant explodes during a safety test. Radioactive fallout over Europe. The disaster damages nuclear power's public standing for decades and reveals the Soviet state's incapacity to handle its own infrastructure — contributing to the regime's collapse five years later.

events.name: Sputnik
events.desc: October 4, 1957. An R-7 rocket lifts off from Baikonur and puts an 84-kilogram aluminum sphere into low Earth orbit, beeping on shortwave every 96 minutes. The American shock is total: the USSR has not only caught up technologically but leapfrogged. NASA is founded within ten months; ARPA (later DARPA) within six; the National Defense Education Act pours federal money into physics, math, and foreign-language training. The space race, the missile-gap panic, and the computing revolution that will end the USSR all begin with this single radio tone.

events.name: Intel founded
events.desc: Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore leave Fairchild Semiconductor and start Intel in Mountain View. Moore has already published his law — transistor counts doubling every two years. Intel ships the first DRAM in 1970, the first microprocessor (the 4004) in 1971, and by the 1990s is the most valuable semiconductor company on earth. The 'Intel Inside' PC era defines three decades of computing. The company's later stumble against Nvidia and TSMC becomes one of the great industrial stories of the 2020s.

events.name: TSMC founded
events.desc: Morris Chang founds Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company in Hsinchu Science Park as a pure-play foundry — a company that only manufactures chips designed by others. The model is initially dismissed; it becomes the foundation of the modern semiconductor industry. By 2025 TSMC fabricates over 90 percent of the world's most advanced logic chips, including every leading-edge Apple, AMD, Nvidia, and Broadcom product. The Taiwan Strait becomes the single most important choke point in the global economy — the 'silicon shield' underwriting Taiwanese sovereignty and locking American and Chinese strategic interests into direct confrontation.

events.name: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
events.desc: May 11, 1997, in midtown Manhattan. IBM's Deep Blue defeats world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3½–2½ in a six-game rematch. The first time a computer has beaten a reigning world champion at classical chess under tournament conditions. Kasparov, shaken, accuses IBM of cheating; IBM retires the machine. The symbolic threshold — the moment when a computer beats the best human at the West's canonical game of pure intellect — predates the deep-learning revolution by a decade and a half, but establishes the narrative template that AlphaGo and ChatGPT will inherit.

events.name: Hong Kong handover
events.desc: July 1, 1997, midnight. Prince Charles and Chris Patten board HMY Britannia and sail out of Victoria Harbour; the Union Jack comes down at Government House. 155 years after the Treaty of Nanking ceded the island to Queen Victoria, Britain returns Hong Kong to the People's Republic of China under the 'one country, two systems' framework promised to preserve the territory's capitalist system and liberties for 50 years. Deng Xiaoping does not live to see it — he dies in February. The world's most successful colonial city becomes the PRC's window on international finance. The framework is formally honored until 2020, when Beijing imposes the National Security Law, ending Hong Kong's distinctive political space a generation early.

events.name: Macau handover
events.desc: December 20, 1999. Portugal returns Macau to China after 442 years — the longest-held European colony in Asia. The handover ceremony is quieter than Hong Kong's two years earlier; Macau has fewer than 450,000 residents and a fraction of Hong Kong's global profile. Over the next two decades Macau is transformed into the world's largest gambling center — casino revenues surpass the Las Vegas Strip by 2006 and reach six times Las Vegas's level at their peak. The last European colonial flag in Asia comes down, ending the era of European territorial presence on the continent that began with Vasco da Gama in 1498.

polities.name: Soviet Union (final years)
polities.desc: Gorbachev's reforms have lost control. The Warsaw Pact is collapsing. Within two years the USSR itself will dissolve into fifteen successor states.
polities.note: The peaceful disintegration of a superpower has no real precedent. The geopolitical consequences are still working themselves out.

polities.name: United States
polities.desc: The unipolar moment is beginning. American power, alliance structures, and ideological confidence are at a historic peak.

polities.name: European Community
polities.desc: Twelve member states. The Maastricht Treaty is three years away. The euro and the eastern enlargement are yet to come.

polities.name: Canada
polities.desc: Mulroney's Progressive Conservatives govern. The Canada–US Free Trade Agreement has just taken effect. Meech Lake, Quebec sovereignty, and NAFTA are the defining internal debates.

polities.name: People's Republic of China
polities.desc: Deng Xiaoping's reforms are a decade old. Tiananmen has just happened. The economic transformation that will redefine the century is underway.

polities.name: Republic of India
polities.desc: Rajiv Gandhi's term is ending. Liberalization is two years away. The license raj will give way to an economy that doubles every decade.

polities.name: Japan
polities.desc: The Nikkei is about to peak. Japan is the world's second-largest economy and the projected challenger to American supremacy. Both projections will prove wrong.

name: The 2000s
desc: The unipolar moment fades. The Asian Financial Crisis, the bursting dot-com bubble, 9/11, the Iraq War, China's WTO accession, the Global Financial Crisis — in a single decade the assumptions of 1989 come apart. Shale oil remakes US energy; smartphones remake daily life; social media remakes politics.

events.name: September 11 Attacks
events.desc: Al-Qaeda hijackers crash aircraft into the World Trade Center and Pentagon. Nearly 3,000 dead. The US response — the 'War on Terror,' the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq — consumes the following two decades and contributes to the end of the unipolar moment.

events.name: China joins WTO
events.desc: December 11, 2001. Fifteen years of negotiation end with China inside the liberal trading system. Manufacturing migrates east at scales no previous globalization wave approached. The US deindustrial Midwest follows; the American middle class stagnates; a third of the world's manufacturing ends up in a single country by 2020.

events.name: Iraq War
events.desc: The United States and a coalition invade Iraq on contested WMD claims. Baghdad falls in three weeks; the insurgency begins in months. Costs — financial, strategic, and moral — contribute to the end of the unipolar moment and the legitimacy of US liberal-internationalist foreign policy.

events.name: iPhone launch
events.desc: Steve Jobs unveils the iPhone at Macworld. Pocket-sized, touchscreen, always-on internet. Within a decade 2 billion people carry one. The attention economy, the creator economy, the surveillance economy — all downstream of this single product.

events.name: Global Financial Crisis
events.desc: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy September 15, 2008. The collapse of a 158-year-old investment bank exposes the rot in US mortgage finance; credit markets freeze worldwide. $10 trillion in global wealth destroyed. The authority of the Anglo-American financial model never fully recovers — and China emerges with reserves to buy at the bottom.

events.name: Shale Revolution breaks out
events.desc: George Mitchell's thirty-year bet on hydraulic fracturing finally cracks the Barnett Shale commercially; the technique spreads to the Bakken and Permian. By 2012 US oil output is rising for the first time in forty years; by 2018 the US is the world's largest producer. The revolution collapses OPEC's pricing power and underwrites American energy independence.

events.name: Arab Spring
events.desc: Mohamed Bouazizi self-immolates in Tunisia December 17, 2010; within months Ben Ali, Mubarak, and Gaddafi have fallen. The moment of democratic possibility in the Arab world. Within five years Syria and Libya are in civil war; Egypt has a new military regime; only Tunisia retains a fragile democracy. Counterrevolution and jihadism capture the decade.

events.name: Facebook era
events.desc: Facebook IPOs at $104 billion. A billion users. The social media model — attention harvested and sold, discourse algorithmically sorted — becomes the infrastructure of public life in democracies. Unintended political consequences follow.

events.name: Three Gorges Dam completed
events.desc: The largest power station on earth by installed capacity — 22.5 GW across 32 turbines, roughly the output of 20 nuclear reactors. 2.3 kilometers of concrete across the Yangtze in Hubei; 1.3 million people relocated; hundreds of archaeological sites submerged. The dam embodies the Chinese developmental state at its ambition: centralized, enormous, indifferent to cost. Completed in 2006, full generating capacity reached in 2012. Flood-control benefits disputed; sedimentation and seismic side-effects ongoing. The 21st-century successor to the Hoover Dam as the emblem of state-built infrastructure.

events.name: International Space Station complete
events.desc: The assembly of the ISS is declared complete in 2011 after 13 years and more than 30 shuttle and Soyuz flights. 420 tonnes of pressurized modules orbiting at 400 kilometers — the largest artificial object ever in space, continuously inhabited since November 2000. A partnership of the US, Russia, Japan, Canada, and ESA that survives the end of the shuttle program, the Ukraine war, and the rise of SpaceX. Scheduled for deorbit around 2031; no successor comparable in scale or international breadth is under construction.

events.name: Belt and Road Initiative
events.desc: Xi Jinping announces the Silk Road Economic Belt at Nazarbayev University in Astana in September 2013, then the Maritime Silk Road a month later in Jakarta. Over the next decade China loans upwards of a trillion dollars across 150 countries for ports, railways, power plants, and telecommunications — the largest infrastructure push in history, bigger than the Marshall Plan in real terms. Hambantota port, Piraeus, Gwadar, the Mombasa–Nairobi railway, and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor all follow. The initiative is simultaneously an export market for Chinese industrial overcapacity, a geopolitical patronage system, and the physical instantiation of Chinese claims to world-system centrality.

events.name: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
events.desc: March 2016 in Seoul. DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players of the modern era, 4–1 in a five-game match. Go, with its 10^170 board states, had been assumed by researchers to be decades away from computer mastery. AlphaGo's Move 37 in Game 2 — a move no human professional considered, a move AlphaGo itself rated as a 1-in-10,000 choice — becomes the symbolic moment when deep reinforcement learning crosses into creativity. Demis Hassabis and DeepMind give the AI buildout a concrete proof of capability six years before ChatGPT makes it legible to the public.

polities.name: United States (hyperpower)
polities.desc: The unipolar moment, winding down. Two wars in the Middle East, a housing bubble that takes down the financial system, and a decade of elite consensus coming unstuck. The Bush-Obama transition masks a deeper continuity: global military commitments, drone warfare, financial-sector rescues, and the cultivation of the Pacific as the new strategic theater.

polities.name: People's Republic of China (rising)
polities.desc: Hu Jintao's China: WTO membership, Olympics 2008, 10 percent annual growth. The world's factory. Xi Jinping takes power in 2012 and ends the era of collective leadership. The assumption that integration breeds convergence fails visibly.

polities.name: European Union (peak)
polities.desc: The euro launches, the Constitution fails, Eastern Europe joins in 2004 and 2007. Peak integration in 2008–09; afterward the sovereign debt crisis, Greek bailouts, and ultimately Brexit (2016) reveal the limits.

polities.name: Russian Federation (Putin era)
polities.desc: Putin stabilizes post-Yeltsin Russia on oil and gas revenues; the 2008 Georgia war and the 2014 annexation of Crimea make the strategic trajectory visible. Europe nevertheless doubles down on Russian pipeline gas until 2022.

polities.name: Gulf States (ascendant)
polities.desc: High oil prices of the 2000s bankroll Dubai's rise as a global financial and logistics hub, Qatar's LNG buildout, and early moves toward Saudi diversification. The region begins its transition from extraction economy to sovereign-wealth-fund-driven diversified investor.

polities.name: Iran (post-reform)
polities.desc: Khatami's reform era (1997–2005) gives way to Ahmadinejad. The nuclear program accelerates; international sanctions tighten. The 2009 Green Movement protests are suppressed.

polities.name: India (reforming)
polities.desc: The Manmohan Singh era: 8 percent growth, IT services, a rising middle class. Modi's BJP takes power in 2014 and shifts the political culture toward Hindu nationalism. India displaces the UK as the world's fifth-largest economy.

polities.name: Brazil (Lula I)
polities.desc: BRIC boom: high commodity prices, Lula's Bolsa Família, Rio 2016 Olympics. The Petrobras corruption scandal will end the era; Bolsonaro's presidency follows.

polities.name: Japan (post-bubble)
polities.desc: The lost decade extends into a lost generation. China overtakes Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. Fukushima in 2011 ends nuclear as a growth option. Abenomics, LDP dominance, the slow reckoning with demography.

polities.name: Somaliland
polities.desc: Former British Somaliland; declared independence from Somalia in 1991.

polities.name: Western Sahara (disputed)
